    Content from Overview: ML on AWS

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • When is cloud compute the right tool for a researcher who already has a cluster or a workstation?
    • What do SageMaker and Bedrock add on top of renting a machine?

    Objectives

    • Compare cloud compute with campus HPC and lab hardware on hardware generation, cost and control.
    • Introduce S3, SageMaker and Bedrock.
    • Preview the two parts of the lesson.

    This episode compares cloud compute with the compute researchers usually already have, then introduces the three AWS services the lesson uses: S3, SageMaker and Bedrock.

    Cloud vs. the cluster down the hall

    Most researchers already have somewhere to run ML, such as a campus HPC cluster, a departmental GPU server, or a lab workstation. How the cloud compares:

    • Buy once and maintain, or rent the latest. A cluster or lab server is bought once, maintained by someone, and used for five or more years with whatever GPUs were current at purchase. Cloud providers offer each new generation soon after release (Blackwell B200 and GB200 today, Vera Rubin announced for cloud deployment in 2026), billed per second and only while a job runs. The largest systems (72-GPU GB200 racks) are liquid-cooled; most campus data centers are air-cooled and cannot host them without a facility upgrade. Owned hardware costs the same busy or idle, so for GPUs that stay busy owning is cheaper, and for bursty research work renting is.
    • Control and data. On-prem gives full control over the software stack, no quotas, no egress charges, and data that never leaves campus. In the cloud you work within quotas and account permissions, and data moved in or out crosses the network. An idle rented GPU costs the same as a busy one, so every job in this lesson has a runtime cap.
    • Efficiency comes from sharing. Two things decide the energy per unit of useful work: how much of the facility’s power reaches the hardware, and how much of the time the hardware is busy. On the first, power usage effectiveness (PUE, total facility power over IT power, 1.0 is perfect) tracks facility scale: AWS reports a global average of 1.14 for 2025, a 2025 survey of US research HPC puts TACC at about 1.15 and MGHPCC near 1.14, while the Uptime Institute’s 2025 survey puts enterprise and colocation data centers at 1.58-1.80, where a departmental server room also sits. On the second, a GPU is only efficient while it is busy. A lab’s own GPUs idle whenever the lab is not training; a campus cluster pools demand across a university and keeps its hardware busier; a cloud provider pools demand across the world and across time zones, so a GPU that one group releases is running someone else’s job minutes later. Providers do not publish GPU utilization, so this part is reasoning rather than data, but a single institution cannot smooth demand the way a global pool can. (PUE figures are self-reported and measure the building, not the GPUs in it.)

    SageMaker and Bedrock

    Amazon SageMaker is AWS’s managed service for machine learning. You write the training or inference script and pick a machine type; SageMaker runs the script on that machine as a job, with the ML frameworks already installed, and shuts the machine down when the job finishes. In practice that means:

    • High-performance compute only when needed: SageMaker lets you develop interactively in lightweight, inexpensive notebook environments (or your own laptop) and then launch training, tuning, or inference jobs on more powerful instance types only when necessary. You pay for expensive compute only while a job runs.

    • Support for custom scripts: Most training and inference scripts can be run using pre-configured estimators or containers that come with popular ML frameworks such as scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Hugging Face already installed. In many cases, you can simply include a requirements.txt file to add any additional dependencies you need. When you need more control, SageMaker also supports fully custom Docker containers, so you can bring your own code, dependencies, and environments for training, tuning, and inference.

    • Flexible compute options: SageMaker lets you easily select instance types tailored to your project needs. For exploratory analysis, use a lightweight CPU (e.g., ml.m5.large). For compute-intensive tasks, such as training deep learning models, you can switch to GPU instances for faster processing. We’ll cover instances more in-depth throughout the lesson (and how to select them), but here’s a preview of the different types:

      • CPU instances (e.g., ml.m5.large — $0.115/hour): Suitable for general ML workloads, feature engineering, and inference tasks.
      • Memory-optimized instances (e.g., ml.r5.2xlarge — approx. $0.65/hour): Best for handling large datasets in memory.
      • GPU instances (e.g., ml.g5.xlarge — $1.41/hour): Optimized for compute-intensive tasks like deep learning training and fine-tuning, offering accelerated processing.
      • For more details, check out the supplemental “Instances for ML” page. We’ll discuss this topic more throughout the lesson. (Prices here and throughout the lesson are us-east-1 on-demand list prices from the AWS price list of 2026-10-16; other regions are the same or within a few percent.)

    • Parallel training and tuning: training jobs can run across several instances for large models and datasets, and hyperparameter tuning jobs run many training jobs in parallel with a few lines of configuration.

    • Ease of orchestration / Simplified ML pipelines: Traditional high-performance computing (HPC) or high-throughput computing (HTC) environments often require researchers to break ML workflows into separate batch jobs, manually orchestrating each step (e.g., submitting preprocessing, training, cross-validation, and evaluation as distinct tasks and stitching the results together later). In SageMaker, a training or tuning job is launched from a notebook with the script, the data location and the instance type, and the orchestration is handled for you.

    • Cost tracking: every job reports its billable seconds, and every resource can be tagged so that the bill can be broken down by project. For many common research workloads SageMaker is cheap. For example, training roughly 100 small to medium-sized models (e.g., logistic regression, random forests, or lightweight deep learning models with a few million parameters) on a small dataset (under 10GB) can cost under $20, making it accessible for many research projects.

    Amazon Bedrock is the other AWS service this lesson uses. Instead of running your script on a machine, Bedrock serves models that AWS hosts through an API. In practice that means:

    • Nothing to start or stop: you call the API and pay per token; when you stop calling it, you stop paying. There is no instance to size, launch, or forget.
    • A catalog of hosted models: DeepSeek, Claude, Amazon’s own models and others, for generation and for embeddings, each selectable by model ID with no download or GPU.
    • Cheap at research scale: embedding a few thousand document chunks and answering a few dozen questions costs cents, which is why the RAG part of the lesson starts here.
    • Only the catalog: if the model you need is not on it, Bedrock cannot serve it. That is the one case where the lesson moves RAG onto SageMaker.
    • Cost tracking by inference profile: Bedrock calls carry no tags by default; the lesson routes them through tagged application inference profiles so they show up on the bill like everything else.

    Amazon S3 is where data lives. Buckets hold files of any size, every SageMaker job reads its inputs from a bucket and writes its outputs back to one, and storage costs about two cents per GB per month. In this lesson you create one bucket of your own in the next episode and use it for the rest of the workshop; the larger datasets are in a shared bucket the instructors staged.

    How the pieces fit together

    Everything in the lesson is one of these four boxes. S3 holds your data and every job’s outputs. The notebook instance is where you work; it is small because it only launches things. SageMaker jobs are where compute happens, on an instance that exists only for the job. Bedrock is an API: no instance at all. Everything the notebook does here can also be done from the AWS command line or from Python on your own machine; the optional last episode shows the CLI equivalents.

    Lesson outline

    The rest of the lesson is hands-on, in two parts:

    1. SageMaker: training, tuning and fine-tuning. Set up an S3 bucket and a small notebook instance, launch training jobs (XGBoost and PyTorch) and a hyperparameter tuning job from it, then fine-tune a vision-language model for handwriting transcription as a training job.
    2. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Build a RAG pipeline over research papers on Amazon Bedrock, then run the same pipeline as SageMaker Processing jobs with an open-weight model.

    Every job is tagged, capped, estimated before launch and checked against the bill after.

    Key Points
    • The cloud offers the current GPU generation on demand and bills per second while a job runs; on-prem hardware offers full control and a fixed cost but a fixed generation and a queue.
    • Renting is cheaper for bursty research work; owning is cheaper for GPUs that stay busy.
    • An idle rented GPU costs the same as a busy one, so every job in this lesson is launched with a runtime cap.
    • SageMaker runs your script in a preconfigured framework container on an instance that exists only for the job; Bedrock serves AWS-hosted models per token with nothing to start or stop.

    Content from Data Storage: Setting up S3

    Last updated on 2026-10-21 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I store and manage data effectively in AWS for SageMaker workflows?
    • What are the best practices for using S3 versus EC2 storage for machine learning projects?

    Objectives

    • Explain data storage options in AWS for machine learning projects.
    • Describe the advantages of S3 for large datasets and multi-user workflows.
    • Create an S3 bucket in the class region with a bucket policy and cost-allocation tags, and upload the Titanic data to it.
    • Estimate S3 storage, transfer and request costs for a small dataset.

    Storing data on AWS

    Machine learning and AI projects rely on data, making efficient storage and management essential. AWS provides several options for storing data, each with different use cases and trade-offs.

    Consult your institution’s IT before handling sensitive data in AWS

    When using AWS for research, ensure that no restricted or sensitive data is uploaded to S3 or any other AWS service unless explicitly approved by your institution’s IT or cloud security team. For projects involving sensitive or regulated data (e.g., HIPAA, FERPA, or proprietary research data), consult your institution’s cloud security or compliance team to explore approved solutions. This may include encryption, restricted-access storage, or dedicated secure environments. If unsure about data classification, review your institution’s data security policies before uploading.

    Options for storage: EC2 Instance or S3

    When working with SageMaker and other AWS services, you have options for data storage, primarily EC2 instances or S3.

    What is an EC2 instance?

    An Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instance is a virtual server: a machine with a chosen amount of CPU, memory, disk and optionally GPU that you rent by the second. Elastic is the point of the name: you can start one, resize it to a different type, add more, and shut them down whenever you want, instead of owning a fixed machine. EC2 instances come in hundreds of types, from small web servers to 8-GPU nodes. Every SageMaker notebook instance and every SageMaker job runs on an EC2 instance underneath; SageMaker’s ml.t3.medium, ml.g5.xlarge and so on are EC2 instance types with an ml. prefix and SageMaker’s software and billing on top.

    When to store data directly on EC2

    Using an EC2 instance for data storage can be useful for temporary or small datasets, especially during processing within a Jupyter notebook. However, this storage is not persistent; if the instance is deleted, the data is erased. (On a SageMaker notebook instance, files under /home/ec2-user/SageMaker survive a Stop and are lost when the instance is Deleted; pip installs and files anywhere else on the instance are lost on every Stop.) Therefore, EC2 is ideal for one-off experiments or intermediate steps in data processing.

    Callout

    Limitations of EC2 storage

    • Scalability: EC2 storage is limited to the instance’s disk capacity, so it may not be ideal for very large datasets.
    • Cost: EC2 storage can be more costly for long-term use compared to S3.
    • Data Persistence: EC2 data may be lost if the instance is stopped or terminated, unless using Elastic Block Store (EBS) for persistent storage. On a SageMaker notebook instance, only /home/ec2-user/SageMaker survives a Stop, and nothing survives a Delete.

    What is an S3 bucket?

    Storing data in an S3 bucket is generally preferred for machine learning workflows on AWS, especially when using SageMaker. An S3 bucket is a container in Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) where you can store, organize, and manage data files. Buckets act as the top-level directory within S3 and can hold a virtually unlimited number of files and folders, making them ideal for storing large datasets, backups, logs, or any files needed for your project. You access objects in a bucket via a unique S3 URI (e.g., s3://your-bucket-name/your-file.csv), which you can use to reference data across various AWS services like EC2 and SageMaker.

    Callout

    Benefits of using S3 (recommended for SageMaker and ML workflows)

    For flexibility, scalability, and cost efficiency, store data in S3 and load it into EC2 as needed. This setup allows:

    • Separation of storage and compute: The most essential advantage. Data in S3 remains accessible even when EC2 instances are stopped or terminated, reducing costs and improving workflow flexibility.
    • Easy data sharing: Datasets in S3 are easier to share with team members or across projects compared to EC2 storage.
    • Integration with AWS services: SageMaker, Lambda, and other AWS services can read directly from and write back to S3, streamlining ML workflows.
    • Scalability: S3 handles large datasets efficiently, enabling storage beyond the limits of an EC2 instance’s disk space.
    • Cost efficiency: S3 storage is generally lower cost than expanding EC2 disk volumes, and you only pay for the storage you use.
    • Data persistence: Unlike EC2 storage, which is lost when an instance is deleted, S3 ensures long-term data availability.

    Recommended approach: S3 buckets

    In order to upload our titanic dataset to an S3 bucket on AWS, we’ll follow the below summary procedure (details follow):

    1. Log in to AWS Console and navigate to S3.
    2. Create a new bucket or use an existing one.
    3. Upload your dataset files.
    4. Use the object URL to reference your data in future experiments.

    Detailed procedure

    1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console
    • Log in to the AWS Console through the sign-in link your instructor emailed you. It looks like https://<org>.awsapps.com/start/#/console?account_id=...&role_name=... and opens the console directly in the workshop account and role after you sign in with your university login. Working on your own account, use the regular console sign-in instead.
    2. Navigate to S3
    • Type “S3” in the search bar
    • Recommended: Select the star icon to save S3 as a bookmark in your AWS toolbar
    • Select S3 - Scalable Storage in the Cloud
    3. Create a new bucket

    Click Create bucket. The form has the sections below; most defaults are right. Change only what is listed.

    General configuration

    • AWS Region: the region your instructor named (in the workshop account, US East (Ohio), us-east-2). This must be the same region your notebook instance and jobs run in.
    • Bucket type: General purpose (the default).
    • Bucket namespace: Global namespace. The console recommends the account Regional namespace, but that appends your account ID, region and -an to every bucket name, which would turn sinkorswim-doejohn into sinkorswim-doejohn-123456789012-us-east-2-an everywhere in the lesson. Global keeps the name as you type it.
    • Bucket name: challenge-lastnamefirstname, all lowercase, e.g. sinkorswim-doejohn: the challenge you are working on (sinkorswim, wattbot2026, badgerscribe, badgercode, …), a hyphen, then your last and first name run together. S3 requires lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only, 3 to 63 characters, starting and ending with a letter or digit. Buckets are the one place AWS forces lowercase; for the notebook instance and the tags we use the same words with capitals, SinkOrSwim and DoeJohn. This is the only bucket you will create in the workshop. Every later episode writes its outputs (trained models, embeddings, predictions) into this same bucket.
    Callout

    Wrong region costs money and breaks jobs

    A SageMaker training or processing job reads only from buckets in its own region; a bucket created elsewhere shows up later as “no such bucket” or “access denied” from the job. Reading data across regions from a notebook does work, but every byte is billed as inter-region transfer (about $0.01-0.02 per GB each way), and a model that reads its training set every epoch pays that on every pass. Check the region before you click Create; it cannot be changed afterwards.

    Object Ownership: leave ACLs disabled (the default). Access is managed through the bucket policy you add in the next step and through IAM roles, which is what AWS recommends.

    Block Public Access settings for this bucket: leave Block all public access on (the default). Nothing in this lesson needs public access; if you ever do, use a policy or a signed URL instead of opening the bucket.

    Bucket Versioning: leave Disable (the default). Versioning keeps every overwritten copy and raises storage costs; it is useful for datasets that change over time, not for this workshop.

    Tags (NOT OPTIONAL): tags are how the bill is broken down by project, person and purpose; this is the one section you must fill in. Add the following three keys, spelled exactly (they are the account’s approved cost-allocation keys, see KB 72454). You will put the same three keys on every resource you create in this lesson.

    • Project: your challenge name (SinkOrSwim, WattBot2026, BadgerScribe, BadgerCode, …), e.g. SinkOrSwim
    • Name: your last and first name run together, e.g. DoeJohn
    • Purpose: one of five fixed values, here Storage

    AWS allows tag values of up to 256 characters made of letters, digits, spaces and + - = . _ : / @, and they are case-sensitive. We use capitalised words with no spaces, and the same spelling on every resource: SinkOrSwim and sinkorswim would be separate rows in Cost Explorer.

    Purpose takes one of five values, so that the bill can be summed by kind of work rather than by individual job. Which job it was is already in the job’s name.

    Purpose Used for
    Storage your bucket
    Notebook the controller notebook instance
    Training training jobs, including the fine-tune
    Tuning hyperparameter tuning jobs
    Inference Bedrock calls, RAG jobs, batch transcription
    Callout

    Why these three keys, and why they must be spelled exactly

    Tags only show up in cost reports if the tag key has been activated as a cost allocation tag at the account level. On UW–Madison’s AWS accounts that activation is done centrally by the Public Cloud team for a fixed list of approved keys, documented at AWS - Tagging with an AWS Account (KB 72454). Name, Project, and Purpose are on that list; ModelSize, Team, project (lowercase) or any other spelling are not, and spend tagged with them is invisible in Cost Explorer. The KB page says it plainly: cut and paste, because any deviation stops the tag from reporting.

    Two more things to know now, because they come up in every later episode:

    • Tags never propagate. Tagging this bucket tags the bucket only. The notebook instance, every training job, processing job and Bedrock inference profile you create later needs its own copy of the same three tags.
    • Outside UW, you activate the keys yourself, once, under Billing and Cost Management → Cost allocation tags. Until you do, the tags exist on the resources but not on the bill.

    Default encryption: leave SSE-S3 (the default). Objects are encrypted at rest with keys S3 manages; KMS keys only matter when you need to control the keys yourself.

    Advanced settings: leave closed.

    Click Create bucket at the bottom.

    4. Edit bucket policy

    Once the bucket is created, the console opens the new bucket’s page (a green “Successfully created bucket” banner at the top, an empty Objects list below). If you land on the bucket list instead, click your bucket’s name. We’ll have to edit our bucket’s policy to allow ourselves proper access to any files stored there (e.g., read from bucket, write to bucket). To set these permissions:

    1. Click the Permissions tab (next to Objects, Metadata, Properties).
    2. Scroll down to Bucket policy and click Edit. Paste the following policy, editing the bucket name “sinkorswim-doejohn” to reflect your bucket’s name and replacing <account-id> with the 12-digit AWS account ID shown at the top right of the console (your instructor will also give it to you)

    JSON 

    {
	"Version": "2012-10-17",
	"Statement": [
		{
			"Effect": "Allow",
			"Principal": {
			    "AWS": [
			        "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/ml-sagemaker-use",
			        "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/ml-sagemaker-bedrock-use"
		        ]
			},
			"Action": [
				"s3:GetObject",
				"s3:PutObject",
				"s3:DeleteObject",
				"s3:ListBucket",
				"s3:ListMultipartUploadParts"
			],
			"Resource": [
				"arn:aws:s3:::sinkorswim-doejohn",
				"arn:aws:s3:::sinkorswim-doejohn/*"
			]
		}
	]
}

    What the policy says, line by line:

    • Principal is who gets access. SageMaker never acts as you; it acts as an IAM role attached to your notebook instance and to every job you launch (the execution role). In the workshop account there are two: ml-sagemaker-bedrock-use, which you will pick when you create your notebook instance in the next episode and which every job inherits, and the older SageMaker-only ml-sagemaker-use, listed so that a notebook created with it still reads the bucket. The <account-id> is the 12-digit number shown next to the account name at the top right of the console.
    • Action is what they may do: read objects, write objects, delete objects, list the bucket’s contents, and list the parts of a large upload in progress.
    • Resource is where: the bucket itself (for listing) and everything in it (/*, for the object actions).

    Without this, the notebook can see the bucket but a job’s TrainingInput fails with “access denied” when it tries to list and download its data.

    Callout

    Doing this on your own account

    Everything above transfers; only the role name changes.

    1. Find your execution role. When you create a notebook instance (next episode) you either pick an existing role or let the console create one, named like AmazonSageMaker-ExecutionRole-20261020T120000. Its ARN is shown on the instance’s page under Permissions and encryption, and looks like arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/service-role/AmazonSageMaker-ExecutionRole-....
    2. Put that ARN in the policy as the only entry under Principal, and your bucket name under Resource.
    3. Or skip the bucket policy by putting sagemaker in the bucket name: the console-created role carries the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess policy, which already grants read and write on any bucket whose name contains sagemaker. A bucket named sinkorswim-doejohn is not covered, which is why the bucket policy is needed at all.

    Either way, access comes from one of two places: the role’s own IAM policy (what the role may do anywhere) or the bucket’s policy (what this bucket allows). In the same account, allowing in either one is enough. The SageMaker execution role documentation covers the role side. UW-Madison researchers can bring questions about roles, policies and accounts to the Public Cloud team’s weekly office hours (Thursdays at 2 pm on Zoom) or email cloud-services@cio.wisc.edu.

    Two buckets appear in this workshop, and this is the only one you create. Your bucket holds the data you bring (the Titanic files, uploaded below) and everything the later episodes produce. The larger datasets for the fine-tuning and RAG episodes (hundreds of scanned letters, a corpus of PDFs) live in a shared, read-only bucket that the instructors stage before class: one copy for everyone, instead of a hundred copies of the same files. You read from it and never upload to it; in the workshop account it is ml-marathon-shared, and the episodes that use it have the name in their first cell.

    5. Upload files to the bucket
    • If you haven’t downloaded these files yet (part of workshop setup), download the data for this workshop: data.zip
      • Extract the zip folder contents (Right-click -> Extract all on Windows; Double-click on mac)
      • Save the two data files (train and test) to a location where they can easily be accessed. E.g., …
        • ~/Downloads/data/titanic/titanic_train.csv
        • ~/Downloads/data/titanic/titanic_test.csv
    • Navigate to the Objects tab of your bucket, then Upload.
    • Add Files (titanic_train.csv, titanic_test.csv) and click Upload to complete. These two files are what the next episodes read: the Accessing S3 episode loads them into a notebook straight from this bucket, and the training and tuning episodes point their jobs at the same two objects.
    6. Take note of S3 URI for your data
    • After uploading a file to S3, click on the file to locate its Object URI (e.g., s3://sinkorswim-doejohn/titanic_train.csv). The Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a unique address that specifies the location of the file within S3. This URI is essential for referencing data in AWS services like SageMaker, where it will be used to load data for processing and model training.

    S3 bucket costs

    S3 bucket storage incurs costs based on data storage, data transfer, and request counts.

    Storage costs

    • Storage is charged per GB per month. Typical: Storing 10 GB costs approximately $0.23/month in S3 Standard ($0.023/GB-month in us-east-1).
    • Pricing Tiers: S3 offers multiple storage classes (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier, etc.), with different costs based on access frequency and retrieval times. Standard S3 fits most purposes.

    Data transfer costs

    • Uploading data to S3 is free.
    • Downloading data (out of S3) incurs charges (~$0.09/GB). Be sure to take note of this fee, as it can add up fast for large datasets.
    • In-region transfer (e.g., S3 to EC2) is free, while cross-region data transfer is charged (~$0.02/GB). This is one reason your bucket and your SageMaker resources must be in the same region.
    • Deleting objects is free.

    Request costs

    Every operation on a bucket is an API request, and each one is billed by count. Two kinds matter: GET ($0.0004 per 1,000), charged every time an object is read, and PUT/LIST ($0.005 per 1,000), charged every time an object is written or a prefix is listed. One request is one object, whatever its size: reading a 5 GB file is one GET; reading 5,000 one-kilobyte files is 5,000 GETs.

    A GET happens whenever code opens an object: pd.read_csv("s3://..."), s3.download_file(...), a training job pulling its input channel (one GET per object in the prefix), a PyTorch Dataset that fetches images from S3 one by one. The last case is the one that bites in ML: a dataset of 100,000 images read once per epoch is 100,000 GETs per epoch, and a 50-epoch run is 5 million requests, about $2. Still small, but no longer zero, and a hyperparameter sweep multiplies it by the number of trials. The usual fix is the one SageMaker already uses for input channels: copy the data to the instance once (File mode) and read it from local disk during training.

    For this lesson, requests round to nothing: two CSVs read a few dozen times. Over a research project, the costs rank in a stable order: storage is the one that accumulates (every dataset, model and output you forget to delete keeps billing monthly), transfer out is the one that spikes (one bulk download of results to a laptop), and requests matter only with many small files read repeatedly.

    To calculate specific costs based on your needs, storage class, and region, refer to AWS’s S3 Pricing Information.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Estimating Storage Costs

    1. Estimate the total cost of storing 1 GB in S3 for one month assuming:

    • Storage duration: 1 month
    • Storage region: us-east-1
    • Storage class: S3 Standard
    • Data will be retrieved 100 times for model training and tuning by SageMaker jobs in the same region (GET requests)
    • Data will be downloaded once to your laptop and then deleted after the project concludes

    Hints

    • S3 storage cost: $0.023 per GB per month (us-east-1)
    • Data transfer cost (download to your laptop): $0.09 per GB (us-east-1 out to internet)
    • In-region transfer (reads by SageMaker jobs): free
    • GET requests cost: $0.0004 per 1,000 requests (each model training will incur one GET request)
    • Deleting objects: free
    • Check the AWS S3 Pricing page for more details.

    2. Repeat the above calculation using the following dataset sizes: 10 GB, 100 GB, 1 TB (1024 GB)

    3. Wrong region. Suppose the 100 GB bucket had been created in us-east-1 but the SageMaker jobs run in us-east-2. The 100 training reads are now cross-region transfers at $0.02 per GB each. What does that add, and how does it compare to the download charge?

    Using the S3 Standard rate in us-east-1:

    1. 1 GB:
      • Storage: 1 GB * $0.023 = $0.023
      • Download: 1 GB * $0.09 = $0.09
      • GET Requests: 100 requests * $0.0004 per 1,000 = $0.00004
      • Deletion: $0
      • Total Cost: $0.11304
    2. 10 GB:
      • Storage: 10 GB * $0.023 = $0.23
      • Download: 10 GB * $0.09 = $0.90
      • GET Requests: 100 requests * $0.0004 per 1,000 = $0.00004
      • Deletion: $0
      • Total Cost: $1.13004
    3. 100 GB:
      • Storage: 100 GB * $0.023 = $2.30
      • Download: 100 GB * $0.09 = $9.00
      • GET Requests: 100 requests * $0.0004 per 1,000 = $0.00004
      • Deletion: $0
      • Total Cost: $11.30004
    4. 1 TB (1024 GB):
      • Storage: 1024 GB * $0.023 = $23.55
      • Download: 1024 GB * $0.09 = $92.16
      • GET Requests: 100 requests * $0.0004 per 1,000 = $0.00004
      • Deletion: $0
      • Total Cost: $115.71004

    These costs assume no additional request charges beyond those for storage, the download, and GET requests for training.

    Two things to notice. The GET line is the same four-thousandths of a cent at every size: request costs depend on how many objects you touch, not how big they are. And the download line grows from 80% of the total at 1 GB to almost all of it at 1 TB: for a dataset of any size, moving it out of AWS costs several times more than keeping it there for a month, so plan to keep large data in the region and bring code to it, not the other way round.

    1. Wrong region, 100 GB: 100 reads x 100 GB x $0.02 = $200 of inter-region transfer, on top of the $11.30 above. The one-time download to a laptop was $9; the misplaced bucket costs twenty times that, silently, and keeps costing with every job. This is why the region is the first setting on the create-bucket form and why the warning above tells you to check it before clicking Create.

    Removing unused data (complete after the workshop)

    After you are done using your data, it’s important to practice good resource stewardship and remove the unneeded files/buckets.

    Option 1: Delete data only (if you plan to reuse bucket for other datasets)

    • Go to S3, navigate to the bucket.
    • Select files to delete, then Actions > Delete.
    • An empty bucket costs nothing: S3 bills for stored bytes and requests, and an empty bucket has neither. Keeping it is fine; the lesson’s end-of-workshop cleanup deletes it only because the shared account is swept between terms.

    Option 2: Delete the S3 bucket entirely (you no longer need the bucket or data)

    • Select the bucket, click Actions > Delete.
    • Type the bucket name to confirm deletion.

    Please complete option 2 following this workshop. On your own account, either option stops the bill: the charges come from the objects, not the bucket.

    Key Points

    • Use S3 for scalable, cost-effective, and flexible storage.

    • EC2 storage is fairly uncommon, but may be suitable for small, temporary datasets; only /home/ec2-user/SageMaker survives a Stop, and nothing survives a Delete.

    • Create the bucket in the same region as your SageMaker notebook, and tag it with the same three keys (Name, Project, Purpose) you will put on every other resource.

    • Track your S3 storage costs, data transfer, and requests to manage expenses.

    • Regularly delete unused data or buckets to avoid ongoing costs.

    Content from Notebooks as Controllers

    Last updated on 2026-10-21 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do you set up and use SageMaker notebooks for machine learning tasks?
    • How can you manage compute resources efficiently using SageMaker’s controller notebook approach?

    Objectives

    • Explain why the lesson works from a SageMaker notebook instance, and what the controller pattern is.
    • Create a tagged notebook instance on a small instance type, open the lesson notebooks in it, and stop it when done.

    Setting up our notebook environment

    In this episode we set up the SageMaker notebook instance that every later episode runs from.

    What a SageMaker notebook instance is

    A SageMaker notebook instance is a virtual machine that AWS runs for you with JupyterLab already installed, a set of Python kernels that come with the AWS SDKs (boto3 and the SageMaker Python SDK), and an IAM role attached that decides what the code running on it may do in your account. You create it from the console and open JupyterLab in a browser tab. Compute is billed per second while it is running and not while it is stopped. The instance’s disk is separate: the files you keep under /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ survive a stop, and that storage volume keeps billing at about $0.14 per GB-month (about $2.80 a month for the 20 GB this lesson asks for) until the instance is deleted.

    Using the notebook as a controller

    The notebook instance is a controller: a small, cheap machine where you write code and use the SageMaker Python SDK to launch larger instances for model training, batch processing, and hyperparameter tuning. Those instances start, run your script, write their results to S3, and shut themselves down, so you pay for powerful hardware only for the minutes a job needs it.

    The notebook is the box on the left of the diagram from the overview episode. Everything else in the picture is launched or called from it, and every later episode uses this same instance.

    Why we work from a notebook instance in this lesson

    The SageMaker SDK runs anywhere Python does, so the lesson could be run from a laptop. We use a notebook instance for four reasons:

    • No credential setup. The IAM role attached to the instance authorizes every call made from it, so there is nothing to install or log in to. Working from a laptop is not hard, aws configure sso and aws sso login take a few minutes, but in a room of a hundred people that is a hundred setups, plus SSO sessions expiring mid-episode and the occasional person pasting an access key instead. The role sidesteps all of it.
    • Everyone has the same environment. The kernels, the SDK version and the paths are identical for every learner, so a cell that works for the instructor works for you.
    • Instructors can see what happened. Every notebook instance in the shared account shows up in the console, and an instructor can open yours and see the notebook that launched a job, with its outputs. Jobs launched from a laptop are just as visible in the job list, but the code that launched them is on your machine, so when something breaks or a charge looks wrong there is less to go on.
    • No egress charges. AWS bills data transfer when it leaves AWS, not when it moves within a region. The notebook instance sits in the same region as your bucket, so reading or downloading files from S3 to the instance is free. Pulling the same files to a laptop costs $0.09 per GB wherever the laptop is: “region” means the AWS data center your resources live in, and a machine outside AWS is never in one.

    We’ll follow these steps to create our first “SageMaker notebook instance”.

    1. Navigate to SageMaker

    • In the AWS Console, search for SageMaker.
    • Recommended: Select the star icon next to Amazon SageMaker AI to save SageMaker as a bookmark in your AWS toolbar
    • Select Amazon SageMaker AI

    2. Create a new notebook instance

    • In the SageMaker left-side menu, click on Notebook instances, then click Create notebook instance.

    • Notebook name: the same words as your bucket, capitalised: Challenge-LastnameFirstname, e.g. SinkOrSwim-DoeJohn. One instance serves the whole workshop; the individual .ipynb notebooks inside it are where the per-episode work lives. SageMaker allows letters, digits and hyphens (no spaces or underscores, up to 63 characters); capitals are fine here and in tags, only bucket names must be lowercase. This name is also reused as the prefix of every training job you launch from the notebook, which is how you will find your jobs in a shared account.

    • Instance type: sets the CPU, memory and price of the virtual machine. Our notebook is a controller, so pick a small one: ml.t3.medium (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, $0.05/hour). The jobs we launch from it will run on more powerful instances; the supplemental Instances for ML page compares them.

    • Platform identifier: This is an internal AWS setting related to the environment version and underlying platform. You can leave this as the default.

    • Additional configuration (leave collapsed): holds the Volume size in GB of the instance’s persistent disk, default 5 GB. Expand it and set 20 GB: the RAG episodes unpack about a gigabyte of PDFs and page images, the fine-tuning episode keeps its data here, and 5 GB fills up on the second run. The disk is the one thing a stopped instance keeps billing for, $0.14 per GB-month, so 20 GB is $2.80 a month until the instance is deleted; do not go larger than that without a reason.

    • Permissions and encryption:

      • IAM role: Select ml-sagemaker-bedrock-use. It is pre-configured for this workshop with access to SageMaker and, for the RAG episodes, Bedrock, with some restrictions to prevent overuse or misuse of resources. The account also has an older ml-sagemaker-use role without the Bedrock permissions; a notebook created with it fails in the Bedrock episode. Outside of the workshop, you create or select a role that includes the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess policy and, for Bedrock, the policy in that episode.
      • Root access: Determines whether the user can run administrative commands within the notebook instance. You should Enable root access to allow installing additional packages if/when needed.
      • Encryption key (skip): While we won’t use this feature for the workshop, it is possible to specify a KMS key for encrypting data at rest if needed.

    • Network (skip): Networking settings are optional. Configure them if you’re working within a specific VPC or need network customization.

    • Git repositories configuration (skip): You don’t need to complete this configuration. Instead, we’ll run a clone command from our notebook later to get our repo setup. This approach is a common strategy (allowing some flexiblity in which repo you use for the notebook).

    • Tags (NOT OPTIONAL): the same three keys you put on your bucket, with the same values except Purpose. Tags never propagate from one resource to another, so the instance needs its own copy; the previous episode’s callout on why these keys and no others applies here too.

      Key Value
      Project your challenge name (SinkOrSwim, WattBot2026, BadgerScribe, BadgerCode, …), e.g. SinkOrSwim
      Name your name, e.g. DoeJohn
      Purpose what this resource is for, Notebook

    • Click Create notebook instance.

    Load pre-filled Jupyter notebooks

    The new instance appears in the list with status Pending. It takes three to five minutes to change to InService, and the Open JupyterLab link does not appear until it does; refreshing the page does not speed it up. Starting a stopped instance later takes about as long. Once it is InService, click Open JupyterLab next to it. In JupyterLab, create a new notebook with the conda_python3 kernel (we aren’t training anything yet, so the plain Python environment is enough).

    In the new notebook, run:

    SH 

    !pwd
!ls

    The first line prints /home/ec2-user/SageMaker: new notebooks start in that folder. The second lists it, and the notebook you just created is the only thing there. SageMaker/ is a separate disk, the volume whose size sits under Additional configuration on the create form (the 20 GB you set). The rest of the instance lives on the system disk and is reset when the instance stops; SageMaker/ is the only place that survives a stop. JupyterLab’s file browser opens there for that reason, and it is where everything in this lesson goes.

    Now clone the lesson repository into it:

    SH 

    !git clone https://github.com/carpentries-incubator/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker.git

    Then open ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.ipynb from the file browser to begin the first notebook.

    At the end of class: stop the instance

    A notebook instance bills for every second it is InService. At the end of class, go to Notebook instances, select yours and choose Stop. Your files under /home/ec2-user/SageMaker (including the repos you clone) survive a Stop and are there when you start it again; packages you pip install are not, so expect to reinstall them. When the workshop is over, Delete the instance: a stopped instance still bills for its storage volume ($0.14 per GB-month), and the cleanup episode walks through this.

    Key Points
    • Use a minimal SageMaker notebook instance as a controller to manage larger, resource-intensive tasks.
    • The notebook does not do the heavy computation; later episodes use it to launch training, tuning and processing jobs on separate instances.
    • Every resource gets the same three tags; they never propagate, so each new resource needs its own.
    • Stop the notebook instance at the end of class, and delete it when the workshop is over.

    Content from Accessing and Managing Data in S3 with SageMaker Notebooks

    Last updated on 2026-10-21 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I load data from S3 into a SageMaker notebook?
    • How do I monitor storage usage and costs for my S3 bucket?
    • What steps are involved in pushing new data back to S3 from a notebook?

    Objectives

    • Read data directly from an S3 bucket into memory in a SageMaker notebook.
    • Check storage usage and estimate costs for data in an S3 bucket.
    • Upload new files from the SageMaker environment back to the S3 bucket.

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.ipynb. Select the conda_python3 kernel (the same one you used in the last episode).

    Set up AWS environment

    To begin each notebook, it’s important to set up an AWS environment that will allow seamless access to the necessary cloud resources. Here’s what we’ll do to get started:

    1. Define the Role: We’ll use get_execution_role() to retrieve the IAM role associated with the SageMaker instance. This role specifies the permissions needed for interacting with AWS services like S3, which allows SageMaker to securely read from and write to storage buckets.

    2. Initialize the SageMaker Session: Next, we’ll create a sagemaker.Session() object, which will help manage and track the resources and operations we use in SageMaker, such as training jobs and model artifacts. The session acts as a bridge between the SageMaker SDK commands in our notebook and AWS services.

    3. Set Up an S3 Client using boto3: Using boto3, we’ll initialize an S3 client for accessing S3 buckets directly. Boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python, allowing developers to interact programmatically with AWS services like S3, EC2, and Lambda.

    Starting with these initializations prepares our notebook environment to efficiently interact with AWS resources for model development, data management, and deployment.

    Start with the role and the session, and print both. The role is the identity every call from this notebook uses. Check the region line against the bucket you made in the S3 episode: the two must match, or the training jobs in later episodes will fail to find their data and anything you do read will be billed as cross-region transfer. If they differ, the fix is a new bucket in this region, not a new notebook instance.

    Work from a project folder beside the lesson clone, so downloads and outputs stay out of the repository. The Titanic episodes all use this one; the fine-tuning and RAG episodes make their own.

    PYTHON 

    !mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic   # a project folder beside the lesson clone, so downloads and outputs stay out of the repository
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic

    PYTHON 

    import sagemaker                      # SageMaker Python SDK: higher-level API for training jobs, tuning, deployment
from sagemaker import get_execution_role

role = sagemaker.get_execution_role() # the IAM role attached to this notebook instance; every call below acts as this role
session = sagemaker.Session()         # tracks the region, default bucket and SageMaker client for this notebook
print(f"Execution Role: {role}")
print(f"AWS Region: {session.boto_region_name}")  # The region of the notebook instance; your bucket must be in this same region
    Callout

    Warnings this cell prints

    sagemaker.config INFO - Not applying SDK defaults from location: ...: an info line, not an error. The SDK looked for an optional defaults file in two standard places and found none.

    SageMakerV2DeprecationWarning: You are using the SageMaker Python SDK v2 ...: the kernels ship SDK v2 and this lesson is written for it. v3 is a rewrite with a different API, so do not install it here. Ignore the warning.

    Next, an S3 client, and a listing of the buckets this role can see.

    PYTHON 

    import boto3                          # AWS SDK for Python: low-level access to every AWS service (S3, EC2, ...)

s3 = boto3.client('s3')               # client for S3 API calls (list, upload, download)
bucket_names = [bucket["Name"] for bucket in s3.list_buckets()["Buckets"]]
print(f"Available S3 Buckets: {bucket_names}")  # Every bucket in the account this role can list, including other learners' buckets in a shared account

    Reading data from S3

    You can either (A) read data from S3 into memory or (B) download a copy of your S3 data into your notebook instance. Since we are using SageMaker notebooks as controllers—rather than performing training or tuning directly in the notebook—the best practice is to read data directly from S3 whenever possible. However, there are cases where downloading a local copy may be useful. We’ll show you both strategies.

    A) Reading data directly from S3 into memory

    This is the recommended approach for most workflows. By keeping data in S3 and reading it into memory when needed, we avoid local storage constraints and ensure that our data remains accessible for SageMaker training and tuning jobs.

    Pros:

    • Scalability: Data remains in S3, allowing multiple training/tuning jobs to access it without duplication.
    • Efficiency: No need to manage local copies or manually clean up storage.
    • Cost-effective: Avoids unnecessary instance storage usage.

    Cons:

    • Network dependency: Requires internet access to S3.
    • Potential latency: Reading large datasets repeatedly from S3 may introduce small delays. This approach works best if you only need to load data once or infrequently.

    Example: Reading data from S3 into memory

    Our data is stored in the S3 bucket you created in the previous episode, named ‘challenge-lastnamefirstname’ (e.g., sinkorswim-doejohn). We can use the following code to read data directly from S3 into memory in the Jupyter notebook environment, without actually downloading a copy of train.csv as a local file.

    PYTHON 

    import pandas as pd
# Define the S3 bucket and object key
bucket_name = 'sinkorswim-doejohn'  # replace with your S3 bucket name

# Read the train data from S3
key = 'titanic_train.csv'  # the object key: the file's path inside the bucket
response = s3.get_object(Bucket=bucket_name, Key=key)  # fetch the object; its bytes arrive as a stream in response['Body']
train_data = pd.read_csv(response['Body'])

# Read the test data from S3
key = 'titanic_test.csv'
response = s3.get_object(Bucket=bucket_name, Key=key)
test_data = pd.read_csv(response['Body'])

# check shape
print(train_data.shape)
print(test_data.shape)

# Inspect the first few rows of the DataFrame
train_data.head()

    B) Download copy into notebook environment

    In some cases, downloading a local copy of the dataset may be useful, such as when performing repeated reads in an interactive notebook session. This download costs nothing: it moves data from S3 to a SageMaker notebook instance in the same region, which AWS does not bill. The same download_file run on your laptop would be a transfer out of AWS at $0.09 per GB.

    Pros:

    • Faster access for repeated operations: Avoids repeated S3 requests.
    • Works offline: Useful if running in an environment with limited network access.

    Cons:

    • Consumes instance storage: Notebook instances have limited space.
    • Requires manual cleanup: Downloaded files remain until deleted.

    Example

    PYTHON 

    !pwd

    PYTHON 

    # Define the S3 bucket and file location
key = "titanic_train.csv"  # Path to your file in the S3 bucket
local_file_path = "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic/titanic_train.csv"  # Local path to save the file

# Copy the object to the instance's disk (unlike get_object above, which only read it into memory)
s3.download_file(bucket_name, key, local_file_path)
!ls "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic/"

    Note: You may need to hit refresh on the file explorer panel to the left to see this file. If you get any permission issues…

    • check that you have selected the appropriate policy for this notebook
    • check that your bucket has the appropriate policy permissions

    Check the current size and storage costs of bucket

    It’s a good idea to periodically check how much storage you have used in your bucket. You can do this from a Jupyter notebook in SageMaker by using the Boto3 library, which is the AWS SDK for Python. This will allow you to calculate the total size of objects within a specified bucket.

    The code below will calculate your bucket size for you. Here is a breakdown of the important pieces in the next code section:

    1. Paginator: Since S3 buckets can contain many objects, we use a paginator to handle large listings.
    2. Size calculation: We sum the Size attribute of each object in the bucket.
    3. Unit conversion: The size is given in bytes, so dividing by 1024 ** 2 converts it to megabytes (MB).

    Note: If your bucket has very large objects or you want to check specific folders within a bucket, you may want to refine this code to only fetch certain objects or folders.

    PYTHON 

    # Initialize the total size counter (bytes)
total_size_bytes = 0

# Use a paginator to handle large bucket listings (one list call returns at most 1000 objects)
# This ensures that even if the bucket contains many objects, we can retrieve all of them
paginator = s3.get_paginator("list_objects_v2")

# Iterate through all pages of object listings
for page in paginator.paginate(Bucket=bucket_name):
    # 'Contents' contains the list of objects in the current page, if available
    for obj in page.get("Contents", []):  
        total_size_bytes += obj["Size"]  # Add each object's size to the total

# Convert the total size to gigabytes for cost estimation
total_size_gb = total_size_bytes / (1024 ** 3)

# Convert the total size to megabytes for easier readability
total_size_mb = total_size_bytes / (1024 ** 2)

# Print the total size in MB
print(f"Total size of bucket '{bucket_name}': {total_size_mb:.2f} MB")

# Print the total size in GB
#print(f"Total size of bucket '{bucket_name}': {total_size_gb:.2f} GB")

    Using the lesson’s helper functions

    We have added code to calculate bucket size to a helper function called get_s3_bucket_size(bucket_name) for your convenience. There are also some other helper functions in scripts/helpers.py of the lesson repository, which you cloned to /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/ in the previous episode.

    Tell Python where the lesson’s scripts/ folder is:

    PYTHON 

    import sys
# Put the lesson's scripts/ folder first on Python's import path
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")
import helpers  # the lesson's helper functions (bucket size, cost estimate, object listing)

    Our helpers.py file can be found in ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/helpers.py. With this file downloaded, you can call this function via…

    PYTHON 

    helpers.get_s3_bucket_size(bucket_name)

    Check storage costs of bucket

    To estimate the storage cost of your Amazon S3 bucket directly from a Jupyter notebook in SageMaker, you can use the following approach. This method calculates the total size of the bucket and estimates the monthly storage cost based on AWS S3 pricing.

    Note: AWS S3 pricing varies by region and storage class. The example below uses the S3 Standard storage class pricing for the US East (N. Virginia) region as of November 1, 2024. Please verify the current pricing for your specific region and storage class on the AWS S3 Pricing page.

    PYTHON 

    # AWS S3 Standard Storage pricing for US East (N. Virginia) region
# Pricing tiers as of November 1, 2024
first_50_tb_price_per_gb = 0.023  # per GB for the first 50 TB
next_450_tb_price_per_gb = 0.022  # per GB for the next 450 TB
over_500_tb_price_per_gb = 0.021  # per GB for storage over 500 TB

# Calculate the cost based on the size
if total_size_gb <= 50 * 1024:
    # Total size is within the first 50 TB
    cost = total_size_gb * first_50_tb_price_per_gb
elif total_size_gb <= 500 * 1024:
    # Total size is within the next 450 TB
    cost = (50 * 1024 * first_50_tb_price_per_gb) + \
           ((total_size_gb - 50 * 1024) * next_450_tb_price_per_gb)
else:
    # Total size is over 500 TB
    cost = (50 * 1024 * first_50_tb_price_per_gb) + \
           (450 * 1024 * next_450_tb_price_per_gb) + \
           ((total_size_gb - 500 * 1024) * over_500_tb_price_per_gb)

print(f"Estimated monthly storage cost: ${cost:.5f}")
print(f"Estimated annual storage cost: ${cost*12:.5f}")

    For your convenience, we have also added this code to a helper function.

    PYTHON 

    monthly_cost, storage_size_gb = helpers.calculate_s3_storage_cost(bucket_name)
print(f"Estimated monthly cost ({storage_size_gb:.4f} GB): ${monthly_cost:.5f}")
print(f"Estimated annual cost ({storage_size_gb:.4f} GB): ${monthly_cost*12:.5f}")

    Important Considerations:

    • Pricing Tiers: AWS S3 pricing is tiered. The first 50 TB per month is priced at $0.023 per GB, the next 450 TB at $0.022 per GB, and storage over 500 TB at $0.021 per GB. Ensure you apply the correct pricing tier based on your total storage size.
    • Region and Storage Class: Pricing varies by AWS region and storage class. The example above uses the S3 Standard storage class pricing for the US East (N. Virginia) region. Adjust the pricing variables if your bucket is in a different region or uses a different storage class.
    • Additional Costs: This estimation covers storage costs only. AWS S3 may have additional charges for requests, data retrievals, and data transfers. For a comprehensive cost analysis, consider these factors as well.

    For detailed and up-to-date information on AWS S3 pricing, please refer to the AWS S3 Pricing page.

    Writing output files to S3

    As your analysis generates new files or demands additional documentation, you can upload files to your bucket as demonstrated below. For this demo, we write a small Notes.txt file on the instance and check that it exists:

    PYTHON 

    notes_file_path = "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic/Notes.txt"
with open(notes_file_path, "w") as f:
    f.write("Workshop notes.\n")

!ls -l "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic/Notes.txt"

    Then upload it. Here it goes under a docs/ prefix; drop the docs/ to put it in the bucket’s root instead.

    PYTHON 

    notes_s3_key = "docs/Notes.txt"   # the object key: a "docs/" prefix plus the file name
# local file -> bucket + key; S3 has no real folders, the "docs/" prefix exists as soon as one key uses it
s3.upload_file(notes_file_path, bucket_name, notes_s3_key)
print(f"Uploaded {notes_file_path} to s3://{bucket_name}/{notes_s3_key}")

    After uploading, we can view the objects/files available on our bucket using…

    PYTHON 

    # List and print all objects in the bucket
response = s3.list_objects_v2(Bucket=bucket_name)  # one page (up to 1000 keys); the paginator above handles more

# Check if there are objects in the bucket
if 'Contents' in response:
    for obj in response['Contents']:
        print(obj['Key'])  # Print the object's key (its path in the bucket)
else:
    print("The bucket is empty or does not exist.")

    Alternatively, we can substitute this for a helper function call as well.

    PYTHON 

    file_list = helpers.list_S3_objects(bucket_name)
file_list
    Challenge

    Challenge: before and after

    1. Using helpers.get_s3_bucket_size(bucket_name), record the size of your bucket. Then create a second file (say docs/Notes2.txt with a few lines of text), upload it under the docs/ prefix, and measure the bucket size again. By how much did it grow, and what does that cost per month at $0.023 per GB?
    2. The next episode launches a training job that writes its outputs to your bucket. Why does the lesson keep everything in one bucket, organised with prefixes like docs/, rather than creating a bucket per task?
    1. One way to do it:

    PYTHON 

    size_before = helpers.get_s3_bucket_size(bucket_name)

with open("Notes2.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("A second note, to see the bucket grow.\n" * 20)
s3.upload_file("Notes2.txt", bucket_name, "docs/Notes2.txt")

size_after = helpers.get_s3_bucket_size(bucket_name)
print(size_before, size_after)

    The bucket grows by the size of the file (a few hundred bytes here), and at $0.023 per GB-month that is well under a thousandth of a cent per month. The same two lines, run before and after a training job, tell you what the job wrote and whether something is accumulating that you should clean up.

    1. A prefix is just part of the object key, so docs/Notes.txt, xgboost/output/... and wattbot/chunks.jsonl can all live in one bucket and still be listed, downloaded or deleted as groups. One bucket means one policy, one set of tags, one region to get right, and one thing to empty and delete at the end; a bucket per task would repeat the setup each time and lengthen the cleanup list.
    Key Points
    • Load data from S3 into memory for efficient storage and processing.
    • Periodically check storage usage and costs to manage S3 budgets.
    • Use SageMaker to upload analysis results and maintain an organized workflow.
    • The lesson repository lives at /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/; every later episode adds its scripts/ folder to sys.path and imports helpers.

    Content from (Optional) Pushing Your Notebooks to GitHub from SageMaker

    Last updated on 2026-10-21 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I put the code I write on a SageMaker notebook instance under version control on GitHub?
    • How do I authenticate to GitHub from a notebook instance without leaving a password or key behind?
    • How can I convert notebooks to .py files and keep .ipynb files out of version control?

    Objectives

    • Create a GitHub repository for your own SageMaker work and connect a folder on the notebook instance to it.
    • Configure Git on a notebook instance to push over HTTPS with a GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT), entered with getpass.
    • Convert .ipynb files to .py files for cleaner version control.

    Open prefilled .ipynb notebook

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/05_Interacting-with-code-repo.ipynb. Select the conda_python3 kernel.

    This episode is optional self-study: it is not needed to run the rest of the lesson, but it is the workflow you will want once you start writing code of your own in SageMaker. It also doubles as a short git refresher. You need a GitHub account for it; nothing else in the lesson does.

    Step 0: What we are versioning, and where

    So far every notebook you have run came from the lesson repository, which you cloned read-only in the notebooks-as-controllers episode. You cannot push to that repository. This episode sets up the usual situation instead: your own work in your own repository. We will create an empty repository on GitHub, make a matching folder on the notebook instance, copy a notebook into it, and push.

    1. On GitHub, click New repository (the + in the top-right corner). Name it sagemaker-work (any name is fine; the cells below use this one). Leave it Public or make it Private, as you prefer. Tick Add a README file so the repository is not empty, which gives Step 6 a pull with something in it. Click Create repository.
    2. Back in JupyterLab, make the folder on the instance and turn it into a git repository. We put it under /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/, the one directory that survives stopping the instance.

    PYTHON 

    %cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/
!mkdir -p sagemaker-work
%cd sagemaker-work
!git init -b main   # start an empty git repository here, with "main" as its first branch

    Connect it to the repository you just created, replacing YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME:

    PYTHON 

    # A remote is a copy of the repository elsewhere; "origin" is the conventional name for the main one (here, GitHub)
!git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/sagemaker-work.git
!git remote -v   # list the remotes and their URLs, to check the address

    Step 1: A GitHub personal access token (PAT)

    A notebook instance is a machine that other people may be able to reach (an administrator, or whoever uses it after you) and that you may delete next month. Neither a saved password nor an SSH key belongs on it. GitHub’s answer is a Personal Access Token: a credential you create with only the permissions you need and an expiry date, use over HTTPS, and revoke in one click. We will enter it with getpass each session so that it never appears in a cell or a saved notebook.

    Important Note: A PAT is a password with a scope. Give it the minimum permissions, set an expiry, and never paste it into code.

    Generate the token on GitHub

    1. Go to Settings by clicking on your profile picture in the upper-right corner of GitHub.
    2. Click Developer settings at the very bottom of the left sidebar.
    3. Select Personal access tokens, then Tokens (classic).
    4. Click Generate new token (classic).
    5. Give it a descriptive name (e.g., “SageMaker notebook instance”) and an expiry (30 days is plenty for a workshop).
    6. Select the minimum permissions needed:
      • For a public repository: only public_repo.
      • For a private repository: repo.
    7. Click Generate token and copy it immediately: you cannot see it again once you leave the page.

    Caution: Treat your PAT like a password. Store it in a password manager, not in a file on the instance, and revoke it (same page, Delete) when the workshop is over; the cleanup episode’s checklist reminds you.

    Enter it with getpass

    input() and getpass.getpass() prompt you in the notebook; the token is held in a Python variable for this kernel session and is not written into the notebook file.

    PYTHON 

    import getpass   # prompts without echoing what you type, so the token never shows on screen or in the saved notebook

username = input("GitHub Username: ")
token = getpass.getpass("GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT): ")  # kept in this variable for the kernel session only

    Note: when you re-run the whole notebook later, this cell prompts again, because nothing is saved.

    Step 2: Configure Git settings

    Git records an author on every commit. Set yours once; --global stores it in your home directory on the instance, so it persists across restarts of this instance (not across instances).

    PYTHON 

    !git config --global user.name "Your name"             # appears as the author in the commit history
!git config --global user.email your_email@example.edu  # use the email on your GitHub account so commits link to your profile

    Step 3: Convert .ipynb to .py

    We want our notebook under version control, but a .ipynb file is JSON with outputs and metadata baked in, which makes diffs unreadable and repositories large. The usual practice is to version a plain .py copy of the code and ignore the notebooks.

    Benefits of converting to .py before committing

    • Cleaner version control: readable diffs, reviewable pull requests, sane merges.
    • Script compatibility: a .py file runs from the command line and imports as a module.
    • Smaller repository: no outputs, no images, no cell metadata.
    1. Install Jupytext, which converts in both directions.

    PYTHON 

    !pip install jupytext   # converts between .ipynb and .py in both directions
    1. Copy the notebook from the Accessing S3 episode into our repository folder (we are still in /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/sagemaker-work) and convert it there. Copying keeps the lesson clone untouched and puts the .py file where git will see it.

    PYTHON 

    # Copy the notebook into the repository folder ("." is the current directory); the lesson clone stays untouched
!cp /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.ipynb .
!jupytext --to py 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.ipynb   # writes a .py next to it: code and markdown, no outputs
    [jupytext] Reading 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.ipynb in format ipynb
[jupytext] Writing 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.py
    1. With several notebooks, convert them all in a loop:

    PYTHON 

    import subprocess
import os

notebooks = [f for f in os.listdir() if f.endswith('.ipynb')]
for notebook in notebooks:
    output_file = notebook.replace('.ipynb', '.py')
    subprocess.run(["jupytext", "--to", "py", notebook, "--output", output_file])  # the same shell command, run from Python
    print(f"Converted {notebook} to {output_file}")

    The same loop is helpers.convert_files() in the lesson’s scripts/helpers.py. It converts every .ipynb in the current directory, so run it from inside the folder you mean to convert:

    PYTHON 

    import sys
# Put the lesson's scripts/ folder on Python's import path, as in the Accessing S3 episode
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")
import helpers
helpers.convert_files(direction="notebook_to_python")

    Step 4: Add and commit the .py file

    1. Check the status of the repository. Make sure you are in the repository folder first.

    PYTHON 

    %cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/sagemaker-work
!git status   # shows the untracked files (the .ipynb and the .py); nothing is staged yet
    1. Add and commit. We add the .py by name rather than git add ., so the .ipynb copy is never tracked (Step 5 ignores it for good).

    PYTHON 

    !git add 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.py   # stage: mark this file to go into the next commit
!git commit -m "Add Accessing-S3 notebook as a script"   # a commit is a snapshot of the staged files; the message says what changed, specifically
    1. Check the status again.

    PYTHON 

    !git status   # the .py is committed; only the untracked .ipynb remains, which Step 5 ignores

    Step 5: Ignore notebooks and clutter with .gitignore

    A .gitignore file lists patterns git should never track. Ignoring *.ipynb across the repository means a stray git add . cannot commit a notebook by accident.

    1. Confirm you are in the repository folder.

    PYTHON 

    !pwd
    1. Create the file (hidden in the file browser because it starts with a dot; ls -a shows it) and add the notebook pattern.

    PYTHON 

    with open(".gitignore", "a") as gitignore:   # "a" appends, so re-running the cell keeps earlier rules
    gitignore.write("# Jupyter notebooks: we version the .py copies instead\n*.ipynb\n")  # one pattern per line; * matches any name
!cat .gitignore
    1. While we are here, ignore the usual clutter too: caches, temporary files, and the NumPy archives the training episodes write next to notebooks.

    PYTHON 

    with open(".gitignore", "a") as gitignore:
    gitignore.write("\n# Cache and temp files\n__pycache__/\n*.tmp\n*.log\n")
!cat .gitignore
    1. Add and commit .gitignore so the rule travels with the repository.

    PYTHON 

    !git add .gitignore   # .gitignore is itself tracked, so everyone who clones gets the same rules
!git commit -m "Ignore notebooks, caches and temp files"

    Step 6: Pull, then push

    Before pushing, pull: the remote already has the README that GitHub created, and in a shared repository it may have your collaborators’ commits. Pulling first means your push is a simple addition rather than a rejected one.

    Which pull strategy

    Git has to decide how to combine your local commits with remote ones. The three options:

    • Merge (pull.rebase false): the remote changes come in as a merge commit. Simplest, shows where you integrated. The default and the right choice for most collaborative work.
    • Rebase (pull.rebase true): your commits are replayed on top of the remote ones, giving a linear history. Cleaner, but conflicts have to be resolved commit by commit.
    • Fast-forward only (pull.ff only): refuses to pull unless nothing diverged. Useful as a safety check, not as a daily setting.

    We use merge. Because our folder and the GitHub repository started separately (one from git init, one from Create repository), git also needs --allow-unrelated-histories for this very first pull; never again after that.

    PYTHON 

    !git config pull.rebase false   # pull strategy: merge (remote commits come in through a merge commit)
# pull = fetch origin's main and merge it into ours; the flag is needed only this once, as the two histories share no commit
!git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories --no-edit

    If git reports a merge conflict, each conflicting file has to be resolved one way or the other and then staged and committed. You will not get one here (the README and your script are different files), but this is what it looks like:

    PYTHON 

    # Example only.
# Keep YOUR version of a file:
# !git checkout --ours 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.py
# Keep the REMOTE version of a file:
# !git checkout --theirs README.md
# Then stage and commit the resolution:
# !git add 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.py README.md
# !git commit -m "Resolve merge conflicts"

    Push with the PAT

    The token goes into the URL for this one command, built from the variables getpass filled. It is not stored by git and does not appear in the notebook.

    PYTHON 

    github_url = f"github.com/{username}/sagemaker-work.git"
# IPython substitutes the Python variables in {braces}; user:token@ in an HTTPS URL authenticates this one push and is not stored
!git push https://{username}:{token}@{github_url} main

    Open https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/sagemaker-work in a browser: the README, the .py file and .gitignore should all be there, with your two commits in the history.

    Step 7: Pulling .py files and converting back to notebooks

    Suppose a collaborator edits the .py file on GitHub, or you edit it from another machine. Pull as usual:

    PYTHON 

    !git config pull.rebase false
!git pull origin main   # a routine pull: no extra flag now that the histories are joined

    Then convert the script back to a notebook with Jupytext. The .ipynb it writes is ignored by git (Step 5), so the round trip leaves the repository clean.

    PYTHON 

    # --to notebook converts the other way; the .ipynb it writes matches the *.ipynb rule in .gitignore
!jupytext --to notebook 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.py --output 04_Accessing-S3-via-SageMaker-notebooks.ipynb

    To convert every .py in the folder back to notebooks, helpers.convert_files(direction="python_to_notebook") does the loop; remember it converts every .py in the current directory, so keep real modules out of that folder.

    Challenge

    Challenge: ignore the big files too

    The training episodes save NumPy arrays (.npz) next to your notebooks. Those are binary and can be large, which makes them a poor fit for git. Add *.npz to your repository’s .gitignore, commit it, push with your PAT, and verify the change on GitHub.

    Still inside /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/sagemaker-work:

    PYTHON 

    with open(".gitignore", "a") as gitignore:
    gitignore.write("\n# NumPy archives saved by the training episodes\n*.npz\n")
!cat .gitignore
!git add .gitignore
!git commit -m "Ignore .npz arrays"
!git push https://{username}:{token}@github.com/{username}/sagemaker-work.git main

    Then open https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/sagemaker-work/blob/main/.gitignore in a browser: the *.npz line should be there, and the commit list should show “Ignore .npz arrays” as the latest commit. If the push is rejected with “authentication failed”, the PAT has expired or lacks the public_repo (or repo) scope; generate a new one and re-run the getpass cell.

    Key Points
    • Your own work belongs in your own repository: create one on GitHub, git init a folder under /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/, and connect the two with git remote add.
    • Authenticate over HTTPS with a scoped, expiring Personal Access Token entered through getpass; nothing is saved on the instance, and the token is revoked when you are done.
    • Version .py copies of notebooks (Jupytext converts both ways) and ignore *.ipynb, caches and data archives in .gitignore.
    • Pull before you push; the first pull into a freshly initialised folder needs --allow-unrelated-histories.

    Content from Training Models in SageMaker: Intro

    Last updated on 2026-10-21 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What are the differences between local training and SageMaker-managed training?
    • How do Estimator classes in SageMaker streamline the training process for various frameworks?
    • How do you estimate what a training job will cost before launching it, and check what it cost afterwards?

    Objectives

    • Understand the difference between training locally in a SageMaker notebook and using SageMaker’s managed infrastructure.
    • Learn to configure and use SageMaker’s Estimator classes for different frameworks (e.g., XGBoost, PyTorch, SKLearn).
    • Tell apart the two ways to run XGBoost on SageMaker, your script in AWS’s container versus AWS’s built-in algorithm in the same container, and know when each fits.
    • Conduct training with data stored in S3 and monitor training job status using the SageMaker console.
    • Estimate the cost of a job before launching it, tag it so it shows up on the bill, and read back its billable time afterwards.

    Initial setup

    1. Open prefilled .ipynb notebook

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/06_Training-models-in-SageMaker-notebooks.ipynb. When asked for a kernel, pick conda_pytorch; we will use the same kernel for the next two episodes. The conda_python3 kernel has no PyTorch, and on current instances no scikit-learn either.

    2. Move to the project folder and import the helpers

    Work from the Titanic project folder the S3 episode created, and make the lesson repository’s scripts/ importable. The training scripts for this episode (train_xgboost.py) and the next (train_nn.py) are in that folder.

    PYTHON 

    # The Titanic project folder from the S3 episode, beside the lesson clone: downloads and outputs land here, not in the repository
!mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic
import sys
# Put the lesson's scripts/ folder on Python's import path
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")
import helpers  # lesson helper functions; train_xgboost.py lives in the same folder

    3. Initialize SageMaker environment

    This code initializes the AWS SageMaker environment by defining the SageMaker role and S3 client. It also specifies the S3 bucket and key for accessing the Titanic training dataset stored in an S3 bucket.

    Boto3 API

    Boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python, allowing developers to interact programmatically with AWS services like S3, EC2, and Lambda. It provides both high-level and low-level APIs, making it easy to manage AWS resources and automate tasks. With built-in support for paginators, waiters, and session management, Boto3 simplifies working with AWS credentials, regions, and IAM permissions. It’s ideal for automating cloud operations and integrating AWS services into Python applications.

    PYTHON 

    import boto3                          # AWS SDK for Python: low-level access to every AWS service (S3, EC2, ...)
import pandas as pd
import sagemaker                      # SageMaker Python SDK: higher-level API for training jobs, tuning, deployment
from sagemaker import get_execution_role

# Initialize the SageMaker role (will reflect notebook instance's policy)
role = sagemaker.get_execution_role()  # the IAM role attached to this notebook instance; every call below acts as this role
print(f'role = {role}')

# Initialize an S3 client to interact with Amazon S3, allowing operations like uploading, downloading, and managing objects and buckets.
s3 = boto3.client('s3')

# Define the S3 bucket that we will load from
bucket_name = 'sinkorswim-doejohn'  # replace with your S3 bucket name

# Define train/test filenames
