!mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")
import helpers

    1. Setup estimator

    To kick off our hyperparameter tuning for a neural network model, we’ll start by defining the SageMaker Estimator. The estimator setup here is very similar to our previous episode, where we used it to configure and train a model directly. However, this time, rather than directly running a training job with the estimator, we’ll be using it as the foundation for hyperparameter tuning.

    In SageMaker, the estimator serves as a blueprint for each tuning job, specifying the training script, instance type, and key parameters like data paths and metrics. Once defined, this estimator will be passed to a Hyperparameter Tuner that manages the creation of multiple training jobs with various hyperparameter combinations, helping us find an optimal configuration.

    Here’s the setup for our PyTorch estimator, which includes specifying the entry script for training (train_nn.py) and defining hyperparameters that will remain fixed across tuning jobs. The hyperparameters we’re setting up to tune include epochs and learning_rate, with a few specific values or ranges defined.

    We’ll use our notebook instance name again to label the training jobs launched in this episode

    PYTHON 

    import boto3

notebook_instance_name = 'SinkOrSwim-DoeJohn' # adjust to your notebook name. we'll use this variable to name the training jobs launched by the tuner.

# the following code just verifies you have the right name for your notebook instance
region = boto3.Session().region_name  # inherited from the notebook instance; do not hard-code a region
sagemaker_client = boto3.client('sagemaker', region_name=region) # Initialize SageMaker client
response = sagemaker_client.describe_notebook_instance(NotebookInstanceName=notebook_instance_name) # Describe the notebook instance

# Display the status and instance type
print(f"Notebook Instance '{notebook_instance_name}' status: {response['NotebookInstanceStatus']}")
local_instance = response['InstanceType']
print(f"Instance Type: {local_instance}")

    Cost tracking: Just like in the previous episode, we explicitly tag each training job at launch time. This ensures that compute usage is traceable to a project, a purpose, and a human-readable name, even after the job has completed. Tags on the HyperparameterTuner are copied to every child training job it launches, so we only need to set them once, on the tuner (we also set them on the estimator so a plain .fit() on it is tagged too).

    PYTHON 

    name = "DoeJohn" # replace with your name
project = "SinkOrSwim" # replace with your challenge name
purpose = "Tuning"        # one of: Storage, Notebook, Training, Tuning, Inference

job_tags = [
    {"Key": "Name", "Value": name},
    {"Key": "Project", "Value": project},
    {"Key": "Purpose", "Value": purpose},
]
print(f"Name: {name}, Project: {project}, Purpose: {purpose}")

    Next, we’ll configure the baseline estimator that we plan to do hyperparameter search on.

    PYTHON 

    import sagemaker
# range types for the search: ContinuousParameter (float range), IntegerParameter (whole-number range), CategoricalParameter (explicit list)
from sagemaker.tuner import HyperparameterTuner, IntegerParameter, ContinuousParameter, CategoricalParameter
from sagemaker.pytorch import PyTorch
from sagemaker.inputs import TrainingInput
from sagemaker import get_execution_role

# Initialize role, bucket, and SageMaker session variables
role = get_execution_role()
bucket_name = 'sinkorswim-doejohn'  # replace with your S3 bucket name
session = sagemaker.Session()
s3 = boto3.client('s3')
print("Role:", role)
print("Region:", session.boto_region_name)

# Define instance type/count we'll use for training
instance_type="ml.m5.large"
instance_count=1 # always start with 1; tuning parallelism comes from max_parallel_jobs, not instance_count
price_per_hour = 0.115 # ml.m5.large, us-east-1 on-demand (2026-10-16); check the instances page for your region

# Define max runtime in seconds to ensure you don't use more compute time than expected. Use a generous threshold (2x expected time but < 2 days) so that work isn't interrupted without any gains.
max_run = 2*60*60 # 2 hours

# Define the PyTorch estimator with entry script and environment details
pytorch_estimator = PyTorch(
    base_job_name=f"{notebook_instance_name}-nn",   # who + which model; the tuner appends its own suffix to each child job
    max_run=max_run, # in seconds; always include (max 48 hours)
    entry_point="/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/train_nn.py",  # Your script for training
    role=role,
    tags=job_tags,  # tags a plain .fit() on this estimator; the tuner below sets its own
    instance_count=instance_count,
    instance_type=instance_type,
    framework_version="2.3",  # if a job fails with an image error, check with: sagemaker.image_uris.retrieve("pytorch", region, version="2.3", py_version="py311", image_scope="training", instance_type="ml.m5.large")
    py_version="py311",
    # the Regex pulls the number out of each "validation:accuracy = 0.8123" line the script prints; SageMaker records it as the metric
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    hyperparameters={
        "train": "/opt/ml/input/data/train/train_data.npz",  # SageMaker will mount this path
        "val": "/opt/ml/input/data/val/val_data.npz",        # SageMaker will mount this path
        "epochs": 100, # Placeholder initial value. Will be overridden by the tuning values tested
        "learning_rate": 0.001 # Placeholder initial value. Will be overridden by the tuning values tested
    },
    sagemaker_session=session,
)

    2. Define hyperparameter ranges

    In SageMaker, you must explicitly define ranges for any hyperparameters you want to tune. SageMaker supports ContinuousParameter, IntegerParameter and CategoricalParameter types:

    • ContinuousParameter allows SageMaker to dynamically sample numeric values within a specified range, making it ideal for broad, exploratory tuning. The total number of values tested can be controlled through the upcoming max_jobs parameter, which defines how many different combinations SageMaker will evaluate.
    • IntegerParameter does the same for whole-number settings such as a batch size or layer width.
    • CategoricalParameter specifies exact values for SageMaker to test, which is useful when you want the model to only try a specific set of options.

    By default, SageMaker uses Bayesian optimization, adjusting future selections based on previous results to efficiently find optimal values. You can also set the strategy to “Random” for uniform sampling across the range, which is effective in larger or more exploratory search spaces. Random sampling may end up costing much more in time and resources, however. Generally, we recommend sticking with the default setting.

    PYTHON 

    # Hyperparameter tuning ranges
hyperparameter_ranges = {
    "epochs": CategoricalParameter([100, 1000, 10000]),       # exact values to try, nothing in between; adjust as needed
    "learning_rate": ContinuousParameter(0.001, 0.1),  # any float in this range; the Bayesian strategy picks where to sample
}

    Hyperparameter considerations in neural nets

    When tuning hyperparameters in neural networks, it’s essential to prioritize parameters that directly impact model performance while remaining mindful of diminishing returns and potential overfitting. Below are some core hyperparameters to consider and general strategies for tuning:

    • Learning Rate: Often the most impactful parameter, learning rate controls the speed of convergence. A smaller learning rate can lead to more stable, though slower, convergence, while a larger rate may speed things up but risks overshooting optimal values. Testing ranges like 0.0001 to 0.1 with a ContinuousParameter is common practice, and Bayesian search can help home in on ideal values.

    • Batch Size: Larger batch sizes often yield faster training times and may improve stability, but this can risk bypassing useful local minima, especially with small datasets. Smaller batch sizes can capture more nuanced updates but are computationally expensive. Ranges from 16 to 256 are worth exploring for most use cases, although, for large datasets or high-capacity models, even larger values may be beneficial.

    • Number of Epochs: While larger epochs allow the model to learn from data longer, increasing epochs doesn’t always equate to better performance and can lead to overfitting. Exploring CategoricalParameter([50, 100, 500, 1000]) can help balance performance without excessive training costs.

    • Layer Width and Depth: Increasing the width or depth (i.e., number of neurons and layers) can improve model capacity but also risks overfitting if the dataset is small or lacks variability. Testing a range of layer sizes or depths (e.g., 32, 64, 128 neurons per layer) can reveal whether additional complexity yields benefits. Notably, understanding double descent is essential here, as larger networks may initially seem to overfit before unexpectedly improving in the second descent—a phenomenon worth investigating in high-capacity networks.

    • Regularization Parameters: Regularization techniques, such as dropout rates or weight decay, can help control overfitting by limiting model capacity. For example, dropout rates from 0.1 to 0.5 or weight decay values of 0.0001 to 0.01 often balance underfitting and overfitting effectively. Higher regularization might inhibit learning, especially if the model is relatively small.

    • Early Stopping: While not a traditional hyperparameter, setting up early stopping based on the validation performance can prevent overfitting without the need to exhaustively test for epoch limits. By allowing the model to halt once performance plateaus or worsens, early stopping can improve efficiency in hyperparameter tuning.

    • Special Phenomena - Grokking and Double Descent: For certain complex datasets or when tuning particularly large models, keep an eye on phenomena like grokking (sudden shifts from poor to excellent generalization) and double descent (an unexpected second drop in error after initial overfitting). These behaviors are more likely to appear in models with high capacity and prolonged training periods, potentially requiring longer epochs or lower learning rates to observe.

    In summary, hyperparameter tuning is a balancing act between expanding model capacity and mitigating overfitting. Prioritize parameters that have shown past efficacy in similar problems, and limit the search to a manageable range—often 20–30 model configurations are sufficient to observe gains. This approach keeps resource consumption practical while achieving meaningful improvements in model performance.

    3. Set up HyperparameterTuner object

    In step 3, we set up the HyperparameterTuner, which controls the tuning process by specifying the…

    • estimator: Here, we connect the previously defined pytorch_estimator to tuner, ensuring that the tuning job will run with our PyTorch model configuration.
    • objective: The metric_definitions and objective_metric_name indicate which metric SageMaker should monitor to find the best-performing model; in this case, we’re tracking “validation:accuracy” and aiming to maximize it. We’ll show you how to setup your training script to report this information in the next step.
    • hyperparameter_ranges: Defined above.
    • strategy: SageMaker uses a Bayesian strategy by default, which iteratively improves parameter selection based on past performance to find an optimal model more efficiently. Although it’s possible to adjust to a “Random” strategy, Bayesian optimization generally provides better results, so it’s recommended to keep this setting.
    • max_jobs and max_parallel_jobs: Finally, we set max_jobs to control the total number of configurations SageMaker will explore and max_parallel_jobs to limit the number of jobs that run simultaneously, balancing resource usage and tuning speed. Since SageMaker tests different hyperparameter values dynamically, it’s important to limit total parallel jobs to <= 4.

    Resource-Conscious Approach: To control costs and energy-needs, choose efficient instance types and limit the search to impactful parameters at a sensible range, keeping resource consumption in check. Hyperparameter tuning often does yield better performing models, but these gains can be marginal after exhausting a reasonable search window of 20-30 model configurations. As a researcher, it’s also important to do some digging on past work to see which parameters may be worthwhile to explore. Make sure you understand what each parameter is doing before you adjust them.

    Always start with max_jobs = 1 and max_parallel_jobs=1. Before running the full search, let’s test our setup by setting max_jobs = 1. This will test just one possible hyperparameter configuration. This critical step helps ensure our code is functional before attempting to scale up.

    PYTHON 

    # Tuner configuration
tuner = HyperparameterTuner(
    base_tuning_job_name=f"{name}-nn-tune"[:20],   # tuning job names are capped at 32 characters and the SDK appends a 12-character timestamp, so the base gets at most 20; child jobs are named <tuning job>-001-<hash>
    estimator=pytorch_estimator,  # the blueprint: every child training job is this estimator with different hyperparameters
    # same regex as the estimator; the value it captures is what the tuner compares across child jobs
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    objective_metric_name="validation:accuracy",  # Ensure this matches the metric name exactly (the "Name" above)
    objective_type="Maximize",                   # Specify if maximizing or minimizing the metric
    hyperparameter_ranges=hyperparameter_ranges,  # the search space defined above
    strategy="Bayesian",  # Default setting (recommend sticking with this!); can adjust to "Random" for uniform sampling across the range
    max_jobs=1,                # Always start with 1 job for debugging purposes. Adjust based on exploration needs (keep below 30 to be kind to environment). 
    max_parallel_jobs=1,         # Always start with 1 for debugging purposes. Recommended to keep this value <= 4 since SageMaker tests values dynamically.
    tags=job_tags,               # propagated to every training job the tuner launches
)

    4. Prepare training script to log metrics

    To prepare train_nn.py for hyperparameter tuning, we added code to log validation metrics in a format that SageMaker recognizes for tracking. In the training loop, we added a print statement for the validation accuracy in a specific format that SageMaker can capture.

    Note: It’s best to use an if statement to only print out metrics periodically (e.g., every 100 epochs), so that your print time does not eat up too much of your training time. It may be a little counter-intuitive that printing can slow things down so dramatically, but it truly does become a significant factor if you’re doing it every epoch. On the flipside of this, you don’t want to print metrics so infrequently that you lose resolution in the monitored validation accuracy. Choose a number between 100-1000 epochs or divide your total epoch count by ~25 to yield a reasonable range.

    if (epoch + 1) % 100 == 0 or epoch == epochs - 1:
    print(f"validation:accuracy = {val_accuracy:.4f}", flush=True)  # Log for SageMaker metric tracking

    Paired with this, our metric_definitions above uses a regular expression "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)" to extract the val_accuracy value from each log line. This regex specifically looks for validation:accuracy =, followed by a floating-point number, which corresponds to the format of our log statement in train_nn.py.

    5. Set data paths and launch tuner.fit()

    In step 5, we define the input data paths for the training job and launch the hyperparameter tuning process. Using TrainingInput, we specify the S3 paths to our train_data.npz and val_data.npz files (uploaded in the previous episode). This setup ensures that SageMaker correctly accesses our training and validation data during each job in the tuning process. We then call tuner.fit and pass a dictionary mapping each data channel (“train” and “val”) to its respective path. This command initiates the tuning job, triggering SageMaker to begin sampling hyperparameter combinations, training the model, and evaluating performance based on our defined objective metric. Once the job is launched, SageMaker handles the tuning process automatically, running the specified number of configurations and keeping track of the best model parameters based on validation accuracy.

    Estimate first: one child job is the same ~1 minute of training plus ~3 minutes of startup we saw in the previous episode, so about $0.01.

    PYTHON 

    # Define the input paths
train_input = TrainingInput(f"s3://{bucket_name}/train_data.npz", content_type="application/x-npz")
val_input = TrainingInput(f"s3://{bucket_name}/val_data.npz", content_type="application/x-npz")

import time as t

# Launch the hyperparameter tuning job (blocks until the single job has finished)
start_time = t.time()
tuner.fit({"train": train_input, "val": val_input})
print(f"Hyperparameter tuning job finished in {t.time() - start_time:.1f} seconds (wall-clock, including instance startup)")

    6. Monitor tuning job from SageMaker console

    While the above cell runs, we can check on the progress by visiting the SageMaker Console and finding the “Training” tab located on the left panel. Click “Hyperparameter tuning jobs” to view running jobs.

    What did that cost?

    The money is spent by the training jobs the tuner launches, and that is where SageMaker records billable time. We bring back job_cost_report() from the previous episodes and run it over every child job of the tuner. The list of child jobs comes from tuner.analytics().dataframe() (one row per training job, with its hyperparameters and final objective value).

    PYTHON 

    def job_cost_report(job_name: str, price_per_hour: float):
    desc = session.sagemaker_client.describe_training_job(TrainingJobName=job_name)
    n = desc["ResourceConfig"]["InstanceCount"]
    billable = desc["BillableTimeInSeconds"] * n
    wall = (desc["TrainingEndTime"] - desc["CreationTime"]).total_seconds()   # launch request to end, including unbilled provisioning
    print(f"{job_name}: status {desc['TrainingJobStatus']}, wall-clock {wall/60:.1f} min, billable {billable/60:.1f} min on {n} instance(s), cost ${billable/3600*price_per_hour:.3f} at ${price_per_hour}/h")
    print(f"    model: {desc['ModelArtifacts']['S3ModelArtifacts']}")   # the model.tar.gz this job uploaded to output_path
    return desc

def tuning_cost_report(tuner, price_per_hour):
    """Call job_cost_report on every training job the tuner launched; return the total cost in dollars."""
    jobs_df = tuner.analytics().dataframe()  # one row per child training job: its hyperparameters, FinalObjectiveValue and TrainingJobName
    total_billable = 0
    for job_name in jobs_df["TrainingJobName"]:
        desc = job_cost_report(job_name, price_per_hour)
        total_billable += desc["BillableTimeInSeconds"] * desc["ResourceConfig"]["InstanceCount"]
    total_cost = total_billable / 3600 * price_per_hour
    print(f"Tuning job {tuner.latest_tuning_job.name}: {len(jobs_df)} training jobs, {total_billable/60:.1f} billable min, ${total_cost:.2f} total")
    return total_cost

tuning_cost_report(tuner, price_per_hour)

    Scaling up our approach

    If all goes well, we can scale up the experiment with the below code. In this configuration, we’re scaling up the search by allowing SageMaker to test more hyperparameter configurations (max_jobs=10) while setting max_parallel_jobs=2 to manage parallelization efficiently. With two jobs running at once, SageMaker will be able to explore potential improvements more quickly than in a fully sequential setup, while still dynamically selecting promising values as it learns from completed jobs. This balance leverages SageMaker’s Bayesian optimization, which uses completed trials to inform subsequent ones, helping to avoid redundant testing of less promising parameter combinations. Setting max_parallel_jobs higher than 2-4 reduces tuning efficiency, as SageMaker’s ability to learn from completed jobs decreases when too many jobs run simultaneously.

    With this approach, SageMaker is better able to refine configurations without overloading resources or risking inefficient exploration, making max_parallel_jobs=2 a solid default for most use cases.

    Estimate first: 10 child jobs at roughly 3 billable minutes each is about 30 billable minutes on ml.m5.large, so about $0.06 in total. Wall-clock is five rounds of two jobs, so expect 15-20 minutes. Write both numbers down; the bill below comes in well under them, for a reason worth knowing.

    PYTHON 

    import time as t # always a good idea to keep a runtime of your experiments 

# Configuration variables
max_jobs = 10
max_parallel_jobs = 2

# Define the Tuner configuration
tuner = HyperparameterTuner(
    base_tuning_job_name=f"{name}-nn-tune"[:20],   # tuning job names are capped at 32 characters and the SDK appends a 12-character timestamp, so the base gets at most 20; child jobs are named <tuning job>-001-<hash>
    estimator=pytorch_estimator,
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    objective_metric_name="validation:accuracy",  # Ensure this matches the metric name exactly
    objective_type="Maximize",                   # Specify if maximizing or minimizing the metric
    hyperparameter_ranges=hyperparameter_ranges,
    max_jobs=max_jobs,
    max_parallel_jobs=max_parallel_jobs,
    tags=job_tags,
)

# Track start time
start_time = t.time()

# Launch the hyperparameter tuning job
tuner.fit({"train": train_input, "val": val_input})

# Calculate runtime
runtime = t.time() - start_time

# Print confirmation with runtime and configuration details
print(f"Tuning runtime: {runtime:.2f} seconds, Instance Type: {instance_type}, Max Jobs: {max_jobs}, Max Parallel Jobs: {max_parallel_jobs}")

    Monitoring tuning

    While the above cell runs, we can check on the progress by visiting the SageMaker Console and finding the “Training” tab located on the left panel. Click “Hyperparameter tuning jobs” to view running jobs.

    • Initial Jobs: SageMaker starts by running only max_parallel_jobs (2 in this case) as the initial batch. As each job completes, new jobs from the remaining pool are triggered until max_jobs (10) is reached.
    • Job Completion: Once the first few jobs complete, SageMaker will continue to launch the remaining jobs up to the maximum of 10, but no more than two at a time.

    Once it has finished, the cost report for all 10 child jobs:

    PYTHON 

    tuning_cost_report(tuner, price_per_hour)

    Our run finished in 9.3 minutes of wall-clock and billed 14.1 minutes in total, $0.03: half the estimate. Read the per-job lines and the reason is visible. The first two child jobs billed about 3 minutes each, like every job so far. The other eight billed about 1 minute each. A tuning job keeps its instances between child jobs, so jobs 3 through 10 ran on the two instances that were already up, with the container pulled and the data downloaded. The startup overhead that dominates a single small job was paid twice, not ten times.

    Can/should we run more instances in parallel?

    Setting max_parallel_jobs to 10 (equal to max_jobs) will indeed launch all 10 jobs in parallel. This approach won’t affect the total cost (since cost is based on the number of total jobs, not how many run concurrently), but it can impact the final results and resource usage pattern due to SageMaker’s ability to dynamically select hyperparameter values to test to maximize efficiency and improve model performance. This adaptability is especially useful for neural networks, which often have a large hyperparameter space with complex interactions. Here’s how SageMaker’s approach impacts typical neural network training:

    1. Adaptive Search Strategies

    • SageMaker offers Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning. Instead of purely random sampling, it learns from previous jobs to choose the next set of hyperparameters more likely to improve the objective metric.
    • For neural networks, this strategy can help converge on better-performing configurations faster by favoring promising areas of the hyperparameter space and discarding poor ones.

    2. Effect of max_parallel_jobs on adaptive tuning

    • When using Bayesian optimization, a lower max_parallel_jobs (e.g., 2–4) can allow SageMaker to iteratively adjust and improve its choices. Each batch of jobs informs the subsequent batch, which may yield better results over time.
    • Conversely, if all jobs are run in parallel (e.g., max_parallel_jobs=10), SageMaker can’t learn and adapt within a single batch, making this setup more like a traditional grid or random search. This approach is still valid, especially for small search spaces, but it doesn’t leverage the full potential of adaptive tuning.

    3. Practical impact on neural network training

    • For simpler models or smaller parameter ranges, running jobs in parallel with a higher max_parallel_jobs works well and quickly completes the search.
    • For more complex neural networks or large hyperparameter spaces, an adaptive strategy with a smaller max_parallel_jobs may yield a better model with fewer total jobs by fine-tuning hyperparameters over multiple iterations.

    Summary

    • For fast, straightforward tuning: Set max_parallel_jobs closer to max_jobs for simultaneous testing.
    • For adaptive, refined tuning: Use a smaller max_parallel_jobs (like 2–4) to let SageMaker leverage adaptive tuning for optimal configurations.

    This balance between exploration and exploitation is particularly impactful in neural network tuning, where training costs can be high and parameters interact in complex ways.

    Extracting and evaluating the best model after tuning

    Tuning takes about 10 minutes to complete — not bad for 10 models! After SageMaker completes the hyperparameter tuning job, the results, including the trained models for each configuration, are stored in an S3 bucket. Here’s a breakdown of the steps to locate and evaluate the best model on test data.

    1. Understanding the folder structure:
      • SageMaker saves each tuning job’s results in the specified S3 bucket under a unique prefix.
      • For the best model, SageMaker stores the model artifact in the format s3://{bucket}/{job_name}/output/model.tar.gz. Each model is compressed as a .tar.gz file containing the saved model parameters.
    2. Retrieve and load the best model:
      • Using the tuner.best_training_job() method, you can get the name of the best-performing job.
      • From there, retrieve the S3 URI of the best model artifact, download it locally, and extract the files for use.
    3. Prepare test data for final assessment of model generalizability
      • Using the scaler that was fit on the training data.
    4. Evaluate the model on test data:
      • Once extracted, load the saved model weights and evaluate the model on your test dataset to get the final performance metrics.

    Here’s the code to implement these steps:

    View best model details and storage info

    We can easily view the best hyperparameters from the tuning procedure…

    PYTHON 

    # 1. Get the best training job from the completed tuning job
best_job_name = tuner.best_training_job()  # the child job with the highest validation:accuracy
print("Best training job name:", best_job_name)

# 2. Use describe_training_job to retrieve full details, including hyperparameters...
best_job_desc = session.sagemaker_client.describe_training_job(TrainingJobName=best_job_name)
best_hyperparameters = best_job_desc["HyperParameters"]
print("Best hyperparameters:", best_hyperparameters)

# ...  and model URI (location on S3)
best_model_s3_uri = best_job_desc['ModelArtifacts']['S3ModelArtifacts']  # the model.tar.gz that job uploaded when it finished
print(f"Best model artifact S3 URI: {best_model_s3_uri}")

    Retrieve and load best model

    Download the winning job’s model.tar.gz and unpack it; SageMaker packs whatever the script saved to /opt/ml/model into that archive.

    PYTHON 

    import tarfile

# Download and extract the model artifact: SageMaker packs whatever the script saved to /opt/ml/model into model.tar.gz
local_model_path = "best_model.tar.gz"
model_bucket, model_key = best_model_s3_uri.split('/')[2], '/'.join(best_model_s3_uri.split('/')[3:])  # s3://bucket/key -> bucket, key
s3.download_file(model_bucket, model_key, local_model_path)

# Extract the model files from the tar.gz archive
with tarfile.open(local_model_path, 'r:gz') as tar:
    tar.extractall()
print("Best model downloaded and extracted.")

    Prepare test set as test_data.npz

    In our previous episode, we converted our train dataset into train/validate subsets, and saved them out as .npz files for efficient processing. We’ll need to preprocess our test data the same way to evaluate it on our model.

    Note: It’s always a good idea to keep preprocessing code as a function so you can apply the same exact procedure across datasets with ease. We’ll import our preprocessing function from train_nn.py, and pass it the scaler that was fit on the training data (saved as scaler.joblib in the previous episode). Calling preprocess_data(test_df) without the scaler would fit a new one on the test set and transform the features differently from what the model saw in training.

    PYTHON 

    !pip install scikit-learn   # train_nn.py imports it; not in the notebook kernels

    Fetch the test CSV and the training-set scaler, transform the test rows the same way the training rows were, and save the arrays.

    PYTHON 

    import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import joblib
from train_nn import preprocess_data

# Fetch the test CSV and the training-set scaler from S3 (both uploaded in earlier episodes)
s3.download_file(bucket_name, "titanic_test.csv", "titanic_test.csv")
s3.download_file(bucket_name, "scaler.joblib", "scaler.joblib")
scaler = joblib.load("scaler.joblib")  # the StandardScaler fit on the training data in the previous episode

# Preprocess test data with the same scaler used for training
test_df = pd.read_csv("titanic_test.csv")
X_test, y_test, _ = preprocess_data(test_df, scaler=scaler)  # transform only; passing the scaler stops it refitting on test data

# Save processed data for testing
np.savez('test_data.npz', X_test=X_test, y_test=y_test)

    Evaluate the model on test data

    Rebuild the network from the script’s class, load the saved weights, and measure accuracy on the test set.

    PYTHON 

    from train_nn import TitanicNet
from train_nn import calculate_accuracy
import torch

# Load the model (saved as 'nn_model.pth' by train_nn.py)
model = TitanicNet()
model.load_state_dict(torch.load("nn_model.pth", map_location="cpu"))
model.eval()

# Load test data
test_data = np.load("test_data.npz")
X_test = torch.tensor(test_data['X_test'], dtype=torch.float32)
y_test = torch.tensor(test_data['y_test'], dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)

# Evaluate the model on the test set
with torch.no_grad():
    predictions = model(X_test)
    accuracy = calculate_accuracy(predictions, y_test)
    print(f"Test Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")

    Conclusions

    In about 10 minutes, we produced a model that is 77-80% accurate on the test set. However, this performance does come at a cost (albeit manageable if you’ve stuck with our advice thus far). This next section will help you assess the total compute time that was used by your tuning job.

    Each child job is billed like any training job; the tuning job itself costs nothing. Here’s a breakdown of what’s happening:

    • Billable Time (BillableTimeInSeconds): the seconds each child job’s instance was yours, from container pull through the script to model upload. The wait for an instance before that is not billed. (TrainingTimeInSeconds is the same number on on-demand instances; it only differs on spot.)

    • Instance Count: billable seconds are multiplied by the number of instances the job used.

    • Per-Second Billing: SageMaker bills per second, with no rounding to minutes or hours. For short jobs like ours, container pull and data download are most of the bill, which is why ten short jobs cost more than one job that trained ten times as long.

    For convenience, we have added this as a function in helpers.py

    PYTHON 

    helpers.calculate_tuning_job_time(tuner, region)  # same per-child-job sum as tuning_cost_report, packaged in helpers.py
    Challenge

    All at once

    Rerun the 10-job search with max_parallel_jobs=10 (equal to max_jobs). Before you launch it, predict what changes in (a) total cost, (b) wall-clock time, and (c) the quality of the search. Then run it and check (a) and (b) with tuning_cost_report() and the runtime print.

    PYTHON 

    tuner_parallel = HyperparameterTuner(
    base_tuning_job_name=f"{name}-nn-tune"[:20],   # tuning job names are capped at 32 characters and the SDK appends a 12-character timestamp, so the base gets at most 20; child jobs are named <tuning job>-001-<hash>
    estimator=pytorch_estimator,
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    objective_metric_name="validation:accuracy",
    objective_type="Maximize",
    hyperparameter_ranges=hyperparameter_ranges,
    max_jobs=10,
    max_parallel_jobs=10,
    tags=job_tags,
)

start_time = t.time()
tuner_parallel.fit({"train": train_input, "val": val_input})
print(f"Tuning runtime: {t.time() - start_time:.2f} seconds with max_parallel_jobs=10")
tuning_cost_report(tuner_parallel, price_per_hour)
print("Best objective, sequential-ish run:", tuner.analytics().dataframe()["FinalObjectiveValue"].max())
print("Best objective, all-parallel run:  ", tuner_parallel.analytics().dataframe()["FinalObjectiveValue"].max())
    • Cost: higher, not the same. Our all-parallel run billed 27.5 minutes ($0.05) against 14.1 minutes ($0.03) for the two-at-a-time run. Ten instances each pull the container and download the data, so the startup overhead is paid ten times; with two at a time it was paid twice and the other eight child jobs reused warm instances. (If your account has a quota on concurrent ml.m5.large training instances, the request may be rejected or throttled, which is the practical limit on this approach.)
    • Wall-clock: roughly one job’s duration. Our run took 4.3 minutes against 9.3, so about twice as fast, not five times: the two-at-a-time run’s later jobs were short because they skipped startup.
    • Search quality: with all 10 launched at once, the Bayesian strategy has no completed results to learn from, so the 10 configurations are effectively a random sample of the space. On a 2-parameter problem this small you will usually see a similar best objective either way; on a larger search space with more jobs, the sequential-ish run tends to find a better configuration for the same number of jobs.
    Challenge

    Tune the batch size too

    Suppose you want to add batch_size to the search as IntegerParameter(16, 256). What has to change in train_nn.py for that to do anything, and what has to change in the notebook?

    The tuner can only vary what the script reads. Right now train_nn.py has no --batch_size argument and trains on the full dataset every epoch (one model(X_train) call per epoch), so a batch_size hyperparameter would be passed on the command line, rejected by argparse, and the job would fail. Three changes are needed:

    1. In train_nn.py: add parser.add_argument('--batch_size', type=int, default=64), pass it to train(), and replace the full-batch step with a mini-batch loop, for example by wrapping the tensors in a TensorDataset and iterating over a DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True) inside each epoch (with optimizer.zero_grad(), forward, loss, backward() and step() per batch).
    parser.add_argument('--batch_size', type=int, default=64)
...
loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X_train, y_train), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
for epoch in range(epochs):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(xb), yb)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    1. In the estimator: add a placeholder "batch_size": 64 to hyperparameters, so the argument is always passed.

    2. In the ranges: add "batch_size": IntegerParameter(16, 256) to hyperparameter_ranges.

    Two side effects worth anticipating: an epoch now takes several optimizer steps instead of one, so the same epochs values train for longer (consider shrinking the epochs choices), and the search space has grown, so 10 jobs will cover it less well; 20-30 would be a reasonable budget, which at these prices is still well under a dollar.

    Key Points
    • Tuner = estimator + ranges + objective: A HyperparameterTuner wraps an ordinary estimator; the script only has to print the objective metric in a format the metric_definitions regex can capture.
    • Start with one job: max_jobs=1, max_parallel_jobs=1 first, to catch script and configuration errors before paying for a search.
    • Parallelism buys time, not quality: Cost is per child training job; max_parallel_jobs changes wall-clock time and, with the Bayesian strategy, how much each job can learn from the ones before it. 2-4 parallel jobs is a good default.
    • Tags propagate from the tuner: Tags on the tuner are copied to every child training job, the one case in SageMaker where tags are inherited.
    • Read the bill from the child jobs: SageMaker bills per second of BillableTimeInSeconds x instance count on each training job; container pull and data download are inside that number and dominate short jobs.
    • Transform the test set with the training scaler: Load the saved scaler and pass it to preprocess_data(test_df, scaler=scaler); never refit on test data.

    Content from Fine-tuning a Vision-Language Model with Training Jobs

    Last updated on 2026-10-21 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • When is fine-tuning worth it?
    • Why does fine-tuning cost anywhere from a dollar to tens of thousands, and how do I estimate where my run falls before I launch it?
    • How do I run a GPU fine-tune as a SageMaker training job so the meter stops the moment it finishes?
    • How do I measure whether the fine-tune helped?

    Objectives

    • Explain what drives the cost of a fine-tuning run (model size × tokens × epochs × number of attempts) and why the same four habits apply at $1 and at $10,000: a time cap, a small first run, and an estimate written down before launch.
    • Launch a LoRA fine-tune of a 3B vision-language model (CHURRO-3B) as a HuggingFace training job on a single 24 GB GPU, with tags, a unique job name and a max_run cap.
    • Read a job’s billable time and compare it to the estimate.
    • Compare the base model and the fine-tuned model on held-out pages using the competition’s own character error rate (CER).
    • Know how to scale the same job up to the full dataset (homework) and to multi-GPU instances for larger models.

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/09_Finetuning-BadgerScribe.ipynb. Select the conda_pytorch kernel.

    Why fine-tune an LLM

    The training episodes so far trained small models from scratch. This episode fine-tunes a large language model with LoRA, the cheap form of fine-tuning explained below: a vision-language model with billions of parameters, pretrained on more data and compute than any lab could repeat. That is what makes it a different kind of job, in what it can do and in what it costs.

    General-purpose models are trained on the average of the internet, and research problems are rarely average. A 19th-century German hand, a lab’s own annotation conventions, species names, a regional dialect, the layout of a specific archive: the largest commercial model has seen little of it, and no prompt can make up for that.

    Done on the right data, a small fine-tuned model beats a much larger general one. The model we LoRA fine-tune in this episode is itself the example: CHURRO, a 3-billion-parameter vision-language model, was fully fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL-3B on about 100,000 pages of historical documents, and its authors report that it exceeds the accuracy of Gemini 2.5 Pro on historical text recognition at 15.5x lower cost (paper). A model that size also runs on one GPU you control, which matters when the data cannot leave your institution, when results have to be reproducible with fixed weights, and when the job is a million pages rather than a demo. CHURRO is not a one-off: the same pattern shows up wherever a research task has its own data.

    Sources: CHURRO, EMNLP 2025; Goedel-Prover-V2, ICLR 2026; MedGemma technical report, 2025. Scores are as reported by each model’s authors.

    The trick

    Fine-tuning is ordinary training that starts from a trained model instead of random weights. You show the model your examples, it computes how wrong its output was, and gradient descent nudges the weights toward your data. Because the model already knows how to read, write and look at images, it needs hundreds of examples to learn your task where training from scratch would need millions. Everything it learned before stays in the weights; you are adjusting them, not replacing them.

    Full fine-tuning is expensive

    Training every weight means storing four numbers per weight instead of one. There is the weight itself, and its gradient, which says which way to nudge it this step. Then there is what the optimizer remembers: Adam, the optimizer everyone uses, keeps for every weight a running average of its recent gradients and a running average of their squares, so that it can give each weight its own step size. And the weight has to be kept in 32-bit as well as 16-bit, because each step’s nudge is far smaller than a 16-bit number can hold; applied to a 16-bit weight it would round away to nothing. Two bytes for the working weight, two for the gradient, four for the 32-bit weight and eight for Adam’s two averages: 16 bytes per parameter, against 2 for inference. A 3B model that runs in 6 GB needs 48 GB to fully fine-tune; a 7B model needs 112 GB, which is already a multi-GPU instance at $25 an hour or more, and the bill scales with every epoch and every retry.

    Do not fully fine-tune anything in this workshop (that is, update all the weights), and do not LoRA fine-tune a model larger than 7B on the class account. A 7B LoRA needs about 22 GB, which is the most the 24 GB GPU the class uses will hold; anything larger needs the 48 GB instance, and above about 13B no instance the account allows holds the model at all. On a few hundred examples a 7B LoRA run is still a few dollars, so retries are cheap. A full fine-tune of a 7B model needs 112 GB, more than any instance the class account allows, and would be a few hundred dollars per run on one that did; a 70B model is $6,000 to $12,000 per run, and a hyperparameter sweep multiplies that by ten. Those runs exist in this episode only as estimates, so that you can recognise one before you launch it.

    LoRA

    LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the pretrained weights and trains a few million extra parameters in small matrices bolted onto the attention and MLP layers. For each large weight matrix W (d × d), it adds two thin ones, B (d × r) and A (r × d), with a rank r of 8 to 64; the layer computes W·x + B·A·x, and only A and B get gradients.

    The frozen weights can stay in 16-bit, since nothing updates them, and the gradients and optimizer state only exist for the adapter. The adapter is about 100 MB, trains on a single 24 GB GPU for a 3B model, and recovers most of the gain of a full fine-tune for a task like this: the model still learns your hands and your conventions, it just learns them through the adapter. This episode uses LoRA.

    Scale, and how easy it is to get wrong

    What makes fine-tuning an LLM different is scale. The training episodes ran for minutes on a $0.12-an-hour CPU; a full fine-tune runs for hours or days on a GPU, a LoRA fine-tune for minutes to hours, and every setting multiplies the bill: model size, epochs, image resolution, instance type, and whether anyone is watching when the job should have ended. Any one of them off by 10x is a 10x bill, and the first run is never the last. Fine-tuning is one of the most common surprise costs we see hurt people, and it is the reason this episode spends as long on estimating and capping a run as on running it. We measure the gain ourselves: the episode ends by scoring the base model and the LoRA fine-tuned model on the same held-out pages.

    The task: Badger Scribe

    Badger Scribe is a Kaggle challenge built from UW Digital Collections material: 19th-century surveyors’ field notebooks, craftsmen’s account books, and German immigrant letters in Kurrent script. Given a page image, produce a verbatim transcription. The score is character error rate (CER): edits per reference character, lower is better.

    This lesson uses the German letters, the Anna Seifert correspondence held by the Max Kade Institute: 191 letters and postcards written between 1932 and 1942 by one woman to her son in Kurrent (the old German handwriting taught in schools until the 1940s, whose letterforms look nothing like today’s cursive: an e is two short strokes, an s can take three shapes, and most Germans alive today cannot read it), transcribed by the Institute’s Kurrent Transcription Group. It is the part of the competition data where every label was produced by a person, and it is most of the hidden test set.

    split pages documents label source
    train 295 4 letter bundles all human-transcribed, ~620 characters per page
    test 141 5 other letter bundles labels held by Kaggle

    Small is the point. 295 labelled pages is a realistic amount of data for a library or a lab to have, and it is enough to move a model that was pre-trained on the right kind of material. Kurrent is also a genuinely different script, not a style of the one the model already reads, so this is a case where the model has to learn something new.

    We LoRA fine-tune CHURRO-3B. It already reads old handwriting across 46 language clusters; we are teaching it these hands and these transcription conventions.

    Step 0: Estimate the cost before you launch anything

    Before launching a fine-tune, write down what it should cost. If the bill is 3x your number, something is wrong, and you want to know on the first run, not the fiftieth.

    What fine-tuning costs, from one dollar to ten thousand

    The cost of a run is GPU-hours × the hourly rate, and GPU-hours scale with model size × tokens seen × epochs, multiplied by how many runs you do before one works. Our class run sits at the very bottom of that curve. The rows below use current SageMaker on-demand prices in us-east-1 (AWS price list, October 2026):

    Run GPUs Instances rented (price per instance-hour) Hours GPU-hours Cost = instance-hours × price
    This episode: 3B LoRA, all 251 Kurrent training pages, 2 passes, 0.7M tokens seen 1 × A10G 1 × ml.g5.xlarge ($1.41) 0.53 0.53 $0.75
    Homework: the same pages, 4 passes, 40 pages scored, 1.4M tokens 1 × A10G 1 × ml.g5.xlarge ($1.41) 1.1 1.1 ~$1.50
    Badger Scribe teams: 3B LoRA, the whole train set (619 pages, all three categories), 2 passes, 1.8M tokens 1 × A10G 1 × ml.g5.xlarge ($1.41) 0.85 0.85 ~$1.20
    7B full fine-tune, 50k documents, 300M tokens (the challenge below) 8 × A100 1 × ml.p4d.24xlarge ($25.25) 5.5 44 ~$140
    70B LoRA, one day 8 × A100 1 × ml.p4d.24xlarge ($25.25) 24 192 ~$600
    CHURRO-3B’s own training: full fine-tune, 100k pages 32 × H100 4 × ml.p5.48xlarge ($63.30) 25 800 ~$6,300
    70B full fine-tune, two days 32 × H100 4 × ml.p5.48xlarge ($63.30) 48 1,536 ~$12,000
    Any row above × a 10-run hyperparameter sweep × 10

    Tokens seen is examples × tokens per example × passes over the data, and it is what the time rule below multiplies by model size. The number of passes is a choice, and the class run’s two passes are a budget choice for a 40-minute job, not a recommendation: large instruction-tuning corpora are usually passed over one to three times, but a few hundred examples usually take three to five. Each extra pass adds one more unit of the same row, so a ten-pass run over the whole train set is about $10, and the sweep row still applies on top. Step 2 shows how the per-epoch curve decides it.

    The class row is measured (2026-10-21: 31.7 billed minutes, $0.75); the homework and teams rows are that run’s seconds per page applied to more passes and pages. The teams row is the competition’s full training set; the shared bucket holds only the German letters, so a team trains on everything from the competition’s own data download.

    GPUs come in fixed boxes: an ml.g5.xlarge is one A10G, an ml.p4d.24xlarge is eight A100s, an ml.p5.48xlarge is eight H100s, and you rent whole boxes. So “32 H100s for 25 hours” is four ml.p5.48xlarge for 25 hours: 100 instance-hours at $63.30 is $6,330. GPU-hours (GPUs × hours) is what the time estimate below produces; divide by the GPUs per box to get instance-hours, and multiply by the box’s price to get the bill.

    Two rows to note. The CHURRO row is the model you are about to LoRA fine-tune: Stanford spent on the order of 800 H100-hours making it, and you get the benefit for a dollar because you are adapting it, not retraining it. Starting from a model that already knows most of the task is the largest cost saving available, and it is decided before any GPU is involved. The sweep row: a first run is rarely the last, so a “$140 full fine-tune” is usually a $700 to $1,400 project. That is the number that surprises research groups. (The 7B row is worked out in the challenge below; the 70B rows are rule-of-thumb magnitudes; the CHURRO figures come from a published review of the paper.)

    The habits in this episode are cheap practice at a dollar a run. At $140 a run they are the difference between a project and a budget incident; at $6,000 a run, one forgotten max_run or one wrong instance type is a grant line.

    Back of the envelope: will it fit, and how long will it take?

    Two rules of thumb answer most of the question before you touch a console. They are good to within a factor of two, which is what you need to tell a $5 run from a $500 one.

    1. Memory: will it fit on the GPU? Count bytes per parameter for what you are doing, multiply by the parameter count, then add a few GB for activations (more for long sequences and big batches).

    What you are doing Bytes per parameter Why 3B 7B 27B 70B
    Inference, 4-bit weights 0.5 weights only 1.5 GB 3.5 GB 14 GB 35 GB
    Inference, FP8 1 weights only 3 GB 7 GB 27 GB 70 GB
    Inference, bf16 2 weights only 6 GB 14 GB 54 GB 140 GB
    LoRA fine-tune ~2.5 frozen bf16 weights + a small adapter with its gradients and optimizer + activations 8 GB 18 GB 68 GB 175 GB
    Full fine-tune, mixed precision 16 16-bit weights 2 + gradients 2 + 32-bit copy of the weights 4 + Adam’s two running averages 8 48 GB 112 GB 430 GB 1.1 TB

    Note the jump from the inference rows to the training rows. Training cannot run on quantized weights the way inference can: each step’s update is too small for 8-bit or 4-bit numbers to hold, so every trained weight keeps a 32-bit copy plus Adam’s two averages, 16 bytes against 2. That is why a 7B model you can run on a 24 GB GPU needs 112 GB plus activations to fully fine-tune, which means several GPUs with the model sharded across them, at $25 to $63 an hour. LoRA sidesteps it by freezing the model and training a few million adapter parameters, which is why this episode fits on one 24 GB card.

    2. Time: how many GPU-hours? Training a token costs three matrix products per layer, each one multiply and one add per weight. Full fine-tuning does all three; LoRA skips the weight update for the frozen base.

    tokens      = examples × tokens per example × passes over the data
FLOPs       = 6 × parameters × tokens      (4 × for LoRA)
GPU-seconds = FLOPs ÷ (GPU peak FLOPS × 0.25)      a real job reaches about a quarter of the data-sheet peak

    Peak FLOPS is on the GPU’s data sheet: about 70 trillion per second for an A10G, 312 for an A100, 989 for an H100. Cost is GPU-hours × the hourly rate, plus about 10 minutes of startup per job.

    The class run: 251 pages × 1,600 tokens × 2 passes = 803k tokens. LoRA on 3.75B parameters: 4 × 3.75e9 × 8.03e5 ≈ 1.2e16 FLOPs. A quarter of an A10G’s 70 TFLOPS is 17 TFLOPS, so about 700 seconds, call it 12 minutes. Measured, the same instance trains at 1.45 seconds per page-pass, so 502 page-passes take about 12 minutes: the rule lands on the number.

    helpers.estimate_finetune_cost does the same arithmetic for any model size, example count, tokens per example and passes. It picks the cheapest instance that fits, or the one you name, and prints memory, GPU-hours, cost per run and per project, and the max_run to set:

    PYTHON 

    import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")
import helpers

helpers.estimate_finetune_cost(
    params_billions=3.75,        # CHURRO-3B: 3B language model + vision tower
    examples=251, tokens_per_example=1600, epochs=2,   # tokens, not words: ~1,300 for the image + ~300 of text; counted in Setup below
    method="lora",
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge",
)

    And on the kind of run a marathon team might be weighing, with the attempts a real project takes:

    PYTHON 

    helpers.estimate_finetune_cost(
    params_billions=7, examples=5000, tokens_per_example=800, epochs=3,
    method="lora", runs=8,       # instance_type=None: the cheapest that fits
)

    tokens_per_example is the input you have to think about, and it is tokens, not words: the model never sees words. Text is about 1.3 tokens per English word, more for German and for old spellings; an image on a Qwen-VL style model is one token per 28 × 28 pixel block after resizing, about 1,300 for a megapixel; for audio, EEG windows or anything else, the model card says what one example becomes. Do not guess it when you can count it: the Setup section below counts the tokens in one page with the model’s own processor. The estimate is good to a factor of two, and it is the number to write down before the launch.

    More GPUs do not make it cheaper. GPU-hours are the cost; spreading them across eight GPUs changes the wall-clock time, not the bill, and only helps if the job is large enough to keep all eight busy. You add GPUs when the memory row above says one GPU cannot hold the job, not to save money.

    Challenge

    Estimate a run you have not launched

    A lab wants to fully fine-tune a 7B model on 50,000 documents of ~2,000 tokens for 3 epochs. They are choosing between ml.p4d.24xlarge (8 × A100 40 GB, $25.25/h, ~312 TFLOPS bf16 per GPU) and renting a single ml.g5.xlarge; the supplemental Instances for ML page has both, with what each box holds and how its price covers all its GPUs. Using the two rules: does it fit on the g5? How many GPU-hours on the p4d, and what does one run cost? What does a realistic project cost?

    It does not fit on the g5: full fine-tuning a 7B model needs ~112 GB plus activations, and the g5 has 24 GB. On the p4d the 8 × 40 GB = 320 GB holds it with the model sharded.

    Tokens: 50,000 × 2,000 × 3 = 3 × 10^8. FLOPs: 6 × 7 × 10^9 × 3 × 10^8 ≈ 1.26 × 10^19. A quarter of an A100’s 312 TFLOPS is 78 TFLOPS: 1.26 × 10^19 / 7.8 × 10^13 ≈ 1.6 × 10^5 GPU-seconds ≈ 45 GPU-hours, which is about 6 hours of wall-clock on 8 GPUs, about $140 for one run (the “7B full fine-tune” row in the table above). The helper gives the same answer:

    PYTHON 

    helpers.estimate_finetune_cost(params_billions=7, examples=50_000, tokens_per_example=2000, epochs=3,
                               method="full", instance_type="ml.p4d.24xlarge",
                               gradient_checkpointing=False, runs=10)

    A realistic project is not one run. The first run finds a data bug, the second a bad learning rate, then two or three are compared, then the one that worked is rerun on the final data: five to ten runs, so $700 to $1,400, before anyone touches a hyperparameter sweep. That is the number to put in the proposal, and it is why the four habits matter more as the model gets bigger.

    The instance

    The model we LoRA fine-tune fits on one 24 GB GPU. Single-GPU and multi-GPU SageMaker training instances, same price list (the full table, with CPU instances and the GPU-by-GPU notes, is on the supplemental Instances for ML page):

    Instance GPU GPU memory $/hour
    ml.g4dn.xlarge 1 × T4 16 GB $0.74
    ml.g6.xlarge 1 × L4 24 GB $1.13
    ml.g5.xlarge 1 × A10G 24 GB $1.41
    ml.g6e.xlarge 1 × L40S 48 GB $2.61
    ml.g5.12xlarge 4 × A10G 96 GB $7.09
    ml.p4d.24xlarge 8 × A100 320 GB $25.25
    ml.p5.48xlarge 8 × H100 640 GB $63.30

    Multi-GPU instances are the right tool when the model, its optimizer state and a batch do not fit on one GPU: a full fine-tune of a 7B model, or anything at 70B. They are the wrong tool when the job does fit on one GPU, because the price goes up 5x to 45x and a job too small to split gets no faster. A 3B LoRA run fits with room to spare, so ml.g5.xlarge is the workhorse for this episode. A T4 is too small and too slow for a 3B vision model with page-sized images; ml.g6.xlarge is a fine substitute if g5 capacity is short; ml.g6e.xlarge is roughly 2–3x faster for less than 2x the price, so it becomes cheaper per run once training outweighs the fixed startup (Exercise 2).

    Scaling the same job to more GPUs

    Nothing in this episode is specific to small runs. The training script uses Hugging Face Trainer, which handles multi-GPU data parallelism when SageMaker launches it under torchrun. To run the same script on a multi-GPU instance, change the estimator, not the script:

    instance_type="ml.p4d.24xlarge",                        # 8 x A100, or ml.g5.12xlarge for 4 x A10G
distribution={"torch_distributed": {"enabled": True}},  # one process per GPU, each on a different slice of the data
max_run=6 * 60 * 60,                                     # 6 hours, in seconds: from the Step 0 estimate, with margin

    Each GPU holds a full copy of the model, so the effective batch becomes batch_size x grad_accum x number of GPUs, and the learning rate usually needs a modest increase. Two lines in the script should be wrapped in if trainer.is_world_process_zero(): so that evaluation and saving run once rather than on every process. When the model, its optimizer state and a batch do not fit on one GPU (a full fine-tune of 7B or more; see the bytes-per-parameter table), data parallelism is not enough: pass fsdp="full_shard" in TrainingArguments (or a DeepSpeed ZeRO config) so the model is sharded across the GPUs, and use instance_count=2 or more for multi-node runs.

    The cost controls do not change with size, but the stakes do. An ml.p4d.24xlarge bills $25.25 an hour and an ml.p5.48xlarge $63.30 an hour from the moment the job starts, and a max_run of six hours is a $150 to $380 ceiling on a single launch. Estimate GPU-hours from the Step 0 rules, set max_run to about twice that estimate, tag the job, and run a slice of the data on one GPU first so that a bug costs a dollar rather than a few hundred. Do not launch a multi-GPU job on the class account.

    The run

    A training job bills from the moment its instance is ready until the job ends, including the minutes spent pulling the container and downloading data and model weights. In class we train on all 251 German-letter training pages for 2 passes and score 15 held-out pages before and after, all inside one job:

    Phase Time Cost
    Waiting for the instance (not billed) ~1 min $0
    Startup: container pull, ~130 MB of images, 7.5 GB of model weights, model load ~5 min $0.12
    Score 15 holdout pages with the base model, ~21 s each ~5 min $0.12
    Training: 251 pages × 2 passes, ~1.5 s per page-pass with gradient checkpointing ~12 min $0.28
    Score 8 of the holdout pages at the end of each pass, ~17 s each, for the curve ~5 min $0.11
    Score the same 15 pages with the LoRA fine-tuned model, ~17 s each ~4 min $0.10
    Save and upload the adapter ~1 min $0.02
    One run ~33 min wall-clock, ~32 min billed $0.75

    Every row is measured, from this exact job run on 2026-10-21: 32.5 minutes from launch to finish, 31.7 billed, $0.75. Scoring a page takes about 17 to 21 seconds, not the 10 a first guess might assume, so the two 15-page evaluations and the curve points are 14 of the 32 minutes: nearly half the bill goes to measuring, not training.

    Training time scales linearly with pages × epochs, and roughly linearly with image resolution (every 28 × 28 pixel block of the page becomes one token in the model’s sequence). Doubling max_pixels doubles the time; doubling epochs doubles it again. Those two settings, left at careless values, are why the estimate must be written down before the first run and compared to the real BillableTimeInSeconds after it.

    We set max_run to about twice the estimate. If a run goes past that, SageMaker kills it and we lose at most a dollar, not a weekend.

    The whole episode

    What Instance Time Cost
    Controller notebook (no GPU needed) ml.t3.medium 3 h $0.15
    LoRA fine-tune on all 251 pages, 2 passes, with before/after scoring and a per-pass curve ml.g5.xlarge ~33 min $0.75
    Exercise 1: same job at 2 megapixels ml.g5.xlarge ~60 min $1.40
    Total ~$2.60

    Compare the classic mistake: doing all of this interactively on a ml.g5.xlarge notebook instance. The class itself costs about the same, but a notebook instance keeps billing after you close the tab. Forgotten over a weekend: $90. Forgotten for a month: $1,029. A training job cannot be forgotten, because it ends.

    Callout

    The four habits

    1. Cap it. Every job gets max_run. Every notebook GPU instance gets stopped when you stand up.
    2. Start small. The first launch of any training script uses a slice of the data and a short cap. The in-class run below is that small first run; the homework scales it up only after it has been seen to work.
    3. Estimate it, then check. Write the number down. After the run, read BillableTimeInSeconds from the job description and compare.
    4. Checkpoint it. Save progress to S3 as the job runs, so that a killed, interrupted or crashed run costs one epoch, not the whole bill.

    Setup

    This episode runs from a CPU notebook instance (ml.t3.medium or ml.m5.xlarge). The notebook is only a controller: it stages data, launches jobs, and reads results. The GPU lives in the job.

    There is no data upload in this episode. The competition data is published as a release on the lesson repository (three zip files: labels, train images, test images), and your instructor has staged it in a shared read-only bucket:

    • s3://<shared-bucket>/badger-scribe/train.csv, test.csv, metadata.csv, metric.py, sample_submission.csv, transcription_conventions.md
    • s3://<shared-bucket>/badger-scribe/images/<page_id>.jpg: train and test pages together, about 130 MB
    • s3://<shared-bucket>/badger-scribe/model/churro-3B/: a copy of the CHURRO-3B weights (~7.5 GB), so that jobs read them from S3 instead of every student pulling them from Hugging Face at once

    The training job reads the images and the model straight from that bucket; the only files your notebook downloads are the small CSVs. Outputs go to your own bucket from the S3 episode, under badger-scribe/.

    The first cell is the same setup as every episode: a SageMaker session, the region and the execution role, and an S3 client. Then the names this episode needs: the shared bucket the jobs read from, your own bucket they write to, your username for job names, and the two S3 prefixes that become the job’s train and model input channels.

    PYTHON 

    import os
import json
import time

import boto3
import pandas as pd
import sagemaker
from sagemaker import get_execution_role

import helpers   # already on sys.path from the Step 0 cell; imported again so Setup runs on its own after a kernel restart

session = sagemaker.Session()
region = session.boto_region_name
role = get_execution_role()
s3_client = boto3.client("s3", region_name=region)
print("Region:", region)
print("Role:", role)

    Now the names, after moving into a project folder of our own under the instance root. Everything this episode downloads or stages (data/, code/) goes there, beside the lesson clone rather than inside it. Two buckets: the shared one the jobs read from, and your own, where everything they write lands. Your username goes into job names, which SageMaker requires to be unique in the account. The two S3 prefixes at the end are what the estimator mounts into the job as its train and model input channels.

    PYTHON 

    !mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/badger-scribe   # a project folder beside the lesson clone, so data and job code stay out of the repository
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/badger-scribe

shared_bucket = "ml-marathon-shared"   # the instructor-staged, read-only bucket with the data and model weights; change only on your own account
bucket_name = "sinkorswim-doejohn"     # <-- EDIT ME: your own bucket from the S3 episode; everything the jobs write goes here
username = "doejohn"                   # <-- EDIT ME: lowercase letters/digits only; used in job names

data_prefix = "badger-scribe"
train_s3_uri = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{data_prefix}/"                  # training channel: csvs + images/
model_s3_uri = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{data_prefix}/model/churro-3B/"  # model channel: staged CHURRO-3B weights

local_data_dir = "./data"
os.makedirs(local_data_dir, exist_ok=True)

    Download the four small files (the two page lists, the metadata and the competition’s scoring script) and look at how the training pages split by category and by who transcribed them.

    PYTHON 

    for fname in ["train.csv", "test.csv", "metadata.csv", "metric.py"]:
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, f"{data_prefix}/{fname}", os.path.join(local_data_dir, fname))

train_df = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(local_data_dir, "train.csv"), keep_default_na=False)   # keep_default_na=False: an empty cell stays "" instead of becoming NaN, so every transcription is a string
test_df = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(local_data_dir, "test.csv"), keep_default_na=False)

print("train pages:", len(train_df), " test pages:", len(test_df))
print(train_df.groupby(["category", "label_source"]).size())

    Not all 295 labelled pages are trained on. The script first sets 15% of them aside, by category and with a fixed seed, so the same 44 pages are held out for every run and every learner; those are the pages every CER in this episode is measured on. The 251 that remain are what the class run trains on, for two passes; the homework trains on the same 251 for four. The holdout is scored three ways: 15 pages before and after training, and 8 of those 15 at the end of every pass. Here are those numbers for this run, from the same settings the training job gets in Step 1:

    PYTHON 

    holdout_frac, eval_pages, curve_pages = 0.15, 15, 8   # the Step 1 hyperparameters that decide the split

n_holdout = round(len(train_df) * holdout_frac)
n_pool = len(train_df) - n_holdout
print(f"{len(train_df)} labelled pages")
print(f"  held out for scoring:   {n_holdout}  ({holdout_frac:.0%}, fixed seed, never trained on)")
print(f"  available for training: {n_pool}")
print(f"  trained on:             all {n_pool}, 2 passes in class, 4 in the homework")
print(f"  scored before/after:    {eval_pages} of the {n_holdout} holdout pages; {curve_pages} of those after every pass")
print(f"test pages (no labels, scored only by Kaggle): {len(test_df)}")

    Look at one page and its transcription. Note what “verbatim” means here: the writer’s spelling and punctuation, umlauts and ß kept as written, Kurrent letterforms mapped to their Latin equivalents, and # for a character the transcriber could not read.

    PYTHON 

    row = train_df[train_df.category == "kade_letters"].iloc[3]
print(row.page_id, "|", row.category, "|", row.label_source)
print(row.text[:600])

    PYTHON 

    from IPython.display import Image, display

page_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, f"{row.page_id}.jpg")
s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, f"{data_prefix}/images/{row.page_id}.jpg", page_path)
display(Image(filename=page_path, width=500))

    How many tokens is a page?

    The cost estimate in Step 0 used 1,600 tokens per page. That number is tokens, not words: the model never sees words. The image becomes one token per 28 × 28 pixel block once it is resized to max_pixels, and the transcription becomes pieces of words, more pieces for German and for old spellings than for modern English. Count it with the model’s own processor rather than guess it; the processor’s files are a few megabytes, so the 7.5 GB of weights stay in S3.

    PYTHON 

    %pip install -q "transformers>=4.56"   # the processor that turns an image + text into the model's tokens; same version as the training job

    Fetch the processor’s config files from the shared bucket and load the processor with the same pixel limits the training script uses. Then run one page through it twice: once with the transcription, to count everything, and once with only the prompt, to find where the transcription’s tokens start. The count splits three ways: the image, the instruction prompt the script sends with every page (the transcription rules from build_prompt plus the chat-template markup around them, the same on every page), and the transcription itself.

    PYTHON 

    from transformers import AutoProcessor
import badger_common as bc

proc_dir = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "churro-processor")
os.makedirs(proc_dir, exist_ok=True)
for fname in ["config.json", "preprocessor_config.json", "tokenizer.json", "tokenizer_config.json", "special_tokens_map.json",
              "added_tokens.json", "vocab.json", "merges.txt", "chat_template.json", "video_preprocessor_config.json"]:
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, f"{data_prefix}/model/churro-3B/{fname}", os.path.join(proc_dir, fname))
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(proc_dir, min_pixels=bc.DEFAULT_MIN_PIXELS, max_pixels=bc.DEFAULT_MAX_PIXELS)

    Now the page you displayed above, prepared exactly as the training script prepares it: the image resized to the pixel cap, the instruction prompt built for its category, and the transcription attached as the assistant’s answer. Running the prompt alone through the processor a second time tells us how many tokens come before the transcription starts.

    PYTHON 

    image = bc.load_page_image(page_path, bc.DEFAULT_MAX_PIXELS)   # resized exactly as the training script resizes it
prompt = bc.build_prompt(row.category)
full = processor.apply_chat_template(bc.full_messages(prompt, row.text), tokenize=False)
enc = processor(text=[full], images=[image], return_tensors="pt")
n_total = enc["input_ids"].shape[1]
n_prompt = processor(text=[processor.apply_chat_template(bc.user_messages(prompt), tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)],
                     images=[image], return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"].shape[1]
n_image = int((enc["image_grid_thw"].prod(dim=1) // 4).sum())   # 14-px patches merged 2x2: one token per 28x28 block

print(f"page {row.page_id}: {image.size[0]} x {image.size[1]} px after resizing -> {n_image} image tokens")
print(f"instruction prompt (same text on every page): {n_prompt - n_image} tokens")
print(f"transcription: {len(row.text.split())} words, {len(row.text)} characters -> {n_total - n_prompt} tokens")
print(f"tokens the model sees for this page: {n_total}")

    Two things to notice in the output. The image is close to the 1,280-token cap whatever the page’s original size, because every scan is larger than a megapixel and gets shrunk to it. And the transcription comes out near two tokens per word, not the 1.3 of the English rule of thumb: German, 1930s spelling and the writer’s abbreviations all split into more pieces. That is why the guess in Step 0 is a guess, and why the next cell measures the average instead.

    One page is a point, not an average. Text length varies a lot from page to page; image tokens hardly vary, because almost every scan is larger than max_pixels and gets resized to the same cap. So count text tokens for every training page with the tokenizer alone, which needs no images and takes seconds, and image tokens over a sample of pages.

    PYTHON 

    text_tokens = train_df.text.map(lambda t: len(processor.tokenizer(t)["input_ids"]))   # every page, tokenizer only

sample = train_df.sample(20, random_state=0)
image_tokens = []
for pid in sample.page_id:
    path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, f"{pid}.jpg")
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, f"{data_prefix}/images/{pid}.jpg", path)
    grid = processor.image_processor(images=[bc.load_page_image(path, bc.DEFAULT_MAX_PIXELS)], return_tensors="pt")["image_grid_thw"]
    image_tokens.append(int((grid.prod(dim=1) // 4).sum()))

    Put the three parts together. The instruction prompt is the same text on every page, so its count from the single page above is reused as a constant.

    PYTHON 

    n_instructions = n_prompt - n_image                      # the instruction prompt: the same text, so the same count, on every page
avg_text, avg_image = text_tokens.mean(), sum(image_tokens) / len(image_tokens)
avg_tokens_per_page = avg_image + n_instructions + avg_text
print(f"text tokens per page, all {len(train_df)} training pages: mean {avg_text:.0f}, min {text_tokens.min()}, max {text_tokens.max()}")
print(f"image tokens per page, {len(image_tokens)} sampled pages: mean {avg_image:.0f}")
print(f"average tokens per page: {avg_image:.0f} image + {n_instructions} instruction prompt + {avg_text:.0f} transcription = {avg_tokens_per_page:.0f}")

    That average is the tokens_per_example the estimate should have used. Re-run the estimator with it and compare with the 1,600 guess:

    PYTHON 

    helpers.estimate_finetune_cost(params_billions=3.75, examples=251, tokens_per_example=int(avg_tokens_per_page), epochs=2,
                               method="lora", instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge")

    Multiply by pages and passes and that is the “tokens seen” in the cost table. Halve max_pixels and the image count halves with it; that is what Exercise 1 changes.

    The scripts

    Jobs run in containers, so the code they execute has to be shipped with the job. Copy the scripts from the lesson repository into a code/ directory:

    PYTHON 

    import shutil

os.makedirs("code", exist_ok=True)
for f in ["badger_common.py", "finetune_churro_lora.py", "churro_transcribe_batch.py"]:
    shutil.copy(f"/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/{f}", f"code/{f}")

with open("code/requirements.txt", "w") as f:  # pip-installed inside the container before the script starts
    f.write("\n".join(["peft>=0.14", "accelerate", "pillow", "pandas"]))

print(os.listdir("code"))
    • badger_common.py: the prompt, image loading, and a copy of the competition’s CER. Shared by the other two so the model is trained on exactly the prompt it is later asked.
    • finetune_churro_lora.py: the training job entry point. Holds out 15% of pages per category, filters to the categories you ask for, scores a sample of holdout pages with the base model, trains a LoRA adapter, scores the same pages again, and saves everything.
    • churro_transcribe_batch.py: used in the homework. Transcribes any list of pages with the base model or with the adapter merged in, and writes predictions.csv in the submission format.

    Open code/finetune_churro_lora.py and read it before launching it. The pieces worth understanding:

    # Only the language model's projection layers get LoRA weights.
# The vision tower ("visual") stays frozen.
lora = LoraConfig(
    r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
    target_modules=r"^(?!.*visual).*\.(q_proj|k_proj|v_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)$",
)

# The loss is computed on the transcription only. Prompt and image tokens
# are masked to -100 so the model is not graded on repeating the question.
labels[i, :n_prompt] = -100

    And the one setting that controls cost more than any other:

    PYTHON 

    # Every 28x28 block of the page becomes one token. 1280 blocks ~ 1 megapixel.
DEFAULT_MAX_PIXELS = 1280 * 28 * 28

    Tags

    As in every episode: tags do not propagate from the notebook to the jobs it launches. Pass them to every estimator.

    PYTHON 

    name = "DoeJohn"         # replace with your name
project = "SinkOrSwim"   # replace with your challenge name

def make_job_tags(purpose: str):   # one of: Storage, Notebook, Training, Tuning, Inference
    return [
        {"Key": "Name", "Value": name},
        {"Key": "Project", "Value": project},
        {"Key": "Purpose", "Value": purpose},
    ]

    Step 1: Launch the LoRA fine-tune

    One job does everything: scores 15 held-out German-letter pages with the base model, trains on the 251 German-letter training pages for 2 passes, scoring 8 of the holdout pages at the end of each pass, scores the same 15 pages again, and saves the adapter. The hyperparameters below are what the Step 0 estimate was built from.

    First the guard rails, each one a named variable so that the printout below shows exactly what the job is allowed to cost and where it saves its progress.

    PYTHON 

    instance_type = "ml.g5.xlarge"            # one A10G GPU, 24 GB; the GPU lives in the job, not in this notebook
g5_price = 1.41                           # $/hour, us-east-1 on-demand
estimated_minutes = 32                    # the Step 0 estimate
max_run_minutes = 65                      # about twice the estimate; SageMaker kills the job at this cap, whatever it is doing
training_job_name = f"badger-{username}-churro-lora-2ep"   # must be unique in the account: a rerun fails instead of launching a second job
checkpoint_s3_uri = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{data_prefix}/checkpoints/{training_job_name}/"   # the script saves the adapter here at the end of every epoch

print(f"job name:     {training_job_name}")
print(f"instance:     {instance_type} at ${g5_price}/h")
print(f"estimate:     {estimated_minutes} min  ->  about ${g5_price * estimated_minutes / 60:.2f}")
print(f"max_run cap:  {max_run_minutes} min  ->  worst case ${g5_price * max_run_minutes / 60:.2f}, then SageMaker stops it")
print(f"checkpoints:  {checkpoint_s3_uri}")
print(f"tags:         {make_job_tags('Training')}")
    Callout

    Four guard rails on every fine-tuning job

    • max_run is the only thing standing between a bug and your whole budget. A training loop that diverges, hangs on a bad batch or waits on a dead data loader bills the same as one that works.
