assert chunk_embeddings.shape[0] == len(chunked_docs), "embeddings and chunks are out of step; delete the cached files and rerun"
print("Embeddings shape:", chunk_embeddings.shape)

    Step 9 – Retrieve: cosine similarity over the embedding matrix

    Retrieval is pure NumPy: embed the question with the same model, take the cosine similarity against every chunk, and keep the top k. retrieve_top_k from wattbot_rag.py does that (open the file to see it: it is a normalize-and-matrix-multiply). No vector database is needed for a few thousand chunks; the optional GPU-notebook episode discusses when one becomes worth it.

    PYTHON 

    first_row = train_df.iloc[0]
print("Sample question:", first_row["question"])

# Cosine similarity of the question vector against every row of the matrix; keep the k best
test_retrieved = retrieve_top_k(embed_query(first_row["question"]), chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs, k=3)
for r in test_retrieved:   # score is the cosine similarity; 1.0 would be an identical vector
    snippet = r["text"].replace("\n", " ")[:160]
    print(f"- score={r['score']:.3f} | doc_id={r['doc_id']} | page={r['page_label']} | {snippet}...")

    Step 10 – Generate: DeepSeek V3 through the converse API

    Bedrock has two runtime APIs. invoke_model takes a provider-specific request body (which is why the Titan call above builds a {"inputText": ...} body by hand). converse is provider-neutral: a system prompt, a list of messages, and an inferenceConfig, in the same shape for DeepSeek, Claude, Llama and the rest. We use converse for generation so the model is a one-line swap. The response carries the generated text and a usage block with the input and output token counts, which is what Bedrock bills on; we keep every usage block so we can price the run at the end.

    PYTHON 

    bedrock_usage = []   # one {"inputTokens": ..., "outputTokens": ...} per call

def call_bedrock_chat(
    system_prompt: str,
    user_prompt: str,
    max_new_tokens: int = 512,
    model_id: str = bedrock_model_id,   # the tagged profile ARN, never the raw model ID
) -> str:
    """Send one system + user turn to a Bedrock chat model and return the generated text."""
    try:
        response = bedrock_runtime.converse(
            modelId=model_id,
            # system: instructions that apply to the whole exchange
            system=[{"text": system_prompt}],
            # messages: the conversation so far, here a single user turn
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": user_prompt}]}],
            # inferenceConfig: generation settings; temperature 0 makes the output repeatable
            inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": max_new_tokens, "temperature": 0},
        )
    except ClientError as e:
        print(f"ERROR calling Bedrock model {model_id}: {e}")
        raise

    bedrock_usage.append(response["usage"])   # token counts for this call, kept so we can price the run later
    # Some models return extra content blocks (e.g. reasoning); keep only the text ones.
    text_blocks = [block["text"] for block in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in block]
    return "\n".join(text_blocks).strip()


print(call_bedrock_chat("You are a concise assistant.", "What is 2 + 2? Answer in one short sentence.", max_new_tokens=32))
print("usage of that call:", bedrock_usage[-1])

    That function has the signature the shared pipeline expects, generate(system_prompt, user_prompt, max_new_tokens) -> str, and embed_query has the other one, embed_query(question) -> vector. Those two callables are the only difference between this episode and the self-hosted ones.

    What the pipeline asks the model

    run_single_qa in wattbot_rag.py makes two calls per question. The first asks for a JSON object in the WattBot submission format, from the retrieved context only; the second, made only when the first produced an answer, asks for a one-to-three-sentence explanation of how the cited material supports it. The system prompt of the first call is the contract that makes the output machine-readable:

    PYTHON 

    print(ANSWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT)

    A question is marked unanswerable (is_blank everywhere, as the competition requires) when the model says so or when the best retrieval score is below retrieval_threshold.

    Step 11 – Run the WattBot evaluation with Bedrock

    Now we can loop over the questions, run retrieval + Bedrock generation, and write a wattbot_solutions_bedrock.csv file (locally and to your bucket).

    train_QA.csv has 245 questions, and at two calls each that is about twenty minutes. For class we score a stratified sample instead: sample_questions_by_type draws ten questions from each evidence type (Quote, Table, Figure, Math, unanswerable, cross-paper, reconcile), about 55 questions after overlaps, so every row of the breakdown in the next step has something in it. The first 55 rows of the file would be nearly all Quote questions. The seed fixes the draw, and the Processing Jobs episode uses the same one, so the two runs are compared on the same questions. Set per_type=0 to run the whole file.

    The Processing Jobs episode reuses this same loop with self-hosted models; the only difference there is that the embedding, answer and explanation phases call local models instead of Bedrock-hosted ones.

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import sample_questions_by_type

eval_df = sample_questions_by_type(train_df, per_type=10, seed=0)   # per_type=0 for all 245
print(f"Scoring {len(eval_df)} of {len(train_df)} questions")

results = []
run_start = time.time()

for _, row in eval_df.iterrows():
    print("#" * 96)
    print(f"QUESTION: {row['question']}")

    out = run_single_qa(
        row=row,                             # one train_QA.csv row: id, question, expected answer_unit
        embed_query=embed_query,             # the two model callables: the only episode-specific inputs
        generate=call_bedrock_chat,
        chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,   # the index: the matrix plus the chunks it was built from
        chunked_docs=chunked_docs,
        docid_to_url=docid_to_url,           # for the ref_url column
        top_k=8,                             # chunks handed to the model as context
        retrieval_threshold=0.25,            # best cosine score below this => unanswerable (is_blank)
        verbose=True,
    )

    print(f"ANSWER: {out['answer']}")
    print(f"ref_ids: {out['ref_id']}")
    print(f"EXPLANATION: {out['explanation']}")
    results.append(out)

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)
print(f"Answered {len(results_df)} questions in {(time.time() - run_start) / 60:.1f} min")

output_dir = "outputs"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)
output_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "wattbot_solutions_bedrock.csv")
results_df.to_csv(output_path, index=False)
s3.upload_file(output_path, bucket_name, solutions_key)
print(f"Wrote predictions to {output_path} and s3://{bucket_name}/{solutions_key}")

results_df.head()

    Step 12 – Score against the training answers

    WattBot scores each prediction with three components: 0.75 for answer_value (numeric within ±0.1% relative tolerance, categorical match after normalisation, and zero if you answer a question the corpus cannot answer), 0.20 for the F1 between your ref_id set and the ground-truth citations, and 0.05 for refusing cleanly, with every evidence field blank, when the answer is is_blank. The number comes from Score.py, the competition’s own metric file, which compute_wattbot_score in wattbot_rag.py calls for the headline score so that what you see here is what the leaderboard would report. It also prints the error rate by evidence type, the seven flag columns of train_QA.csv: Quote (the answer is a sentence in a paper), Table, Figure, Math (a calculation from numbers in the text), is_NA (the corpus cannot answer it, and the right response is is_blank), CrossPaper (numbers from two papers have to be combined) and Reconcile (two figures that sound alike but measure different things, such as water withdrawn against water consumed, or a popular claim against a measured value, and the answer is the ratio or the distinction between them; quoting either figure alone is the wrong answer the question is built to catch). A question can carry several. Read that table before changing anything: figure and table questions failing while quote questions pass points at text extraction, which loses figures and flattens tables, not at the model. The wrapper adds a per-row score, joins on id, and prints the worst-scoring rows so you can see why the pipeline lost points. train_QA.csv has no separate “unanswerable” column, so gt_is_na_col="is_blank" tells the scorer to derive that flag from answer_value == "is_blank" on both sides.

    PYTHON 

    scored_df = compute_wattbot_score(
    train_qa_path=train_qa_path,    # ground truth
    preds_path=output_path,         # our predictions, joined to it on id
    n_examples=20,
)

    Why were the wrong ones wrong?

    The score tells you which questions failed, not why. Two different failures look the same in that table. Either retrieval never surfaced the right paper, so the model had nothing to work with, or the right passage was in front of it and it still declined or misread it. The cell below separates them for the lowest-scoring rows: it joins the model’s own explanation and the passages it cited back onto the score, then reruns retrieval for the question (one embedding call) and reports whether the ground-truth paper was among the top-k chunks and what the best cosine score was.

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import retrieve_top_k, split_ref_ids

worst = scored_df.sort_values("wattbot_score").head(8)
by_id = results_df.set_index("id")   # the model's answer, explanation and cited passages, keyed by question id

for _, row in worst.iterrows():
    qid = row["id"]
    gt_refs = set(split_ref_ids(row["ref_id_gt"]))   # train_QA.csv stores the list as a string
    retrieved = retrieve_top_k(embed_query(row["question_gt"]), chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs, k=8)   # the merge suffixed both sides' columns
    retrieved_docs = [r["doc_id"] for r in retrieved]
    print("=" * 96)
    print(f"{qid}: {row['question_gt']}")
    print(f"  expected: {row['answer_value_gt']}  from {sorted(gt_refs)}")
    print(f"  predicted: {row['answer_value_pred']}  citing {row['ref_id_pred']}")
    print(f"  retrieval: top cosine {retrieved[0]['score']:.3f}; top-8 papers {retrieved_docs}")
    print(f"  ground-truth paper retrieved: {'yes' if gt_refs & set(retrieved_docs) else 'NO'}")
    if by_id.loc[qid, "explanation"] != "is_blank":
        print(f"  model's explanation: {by_id.loc[qid, 'explanation']}")
        print(f"  passages it cited: {str(by_id.loc[qid, 'supporting_materials'])[:400]}")

    Read the two lines at the bottom of each block together. “Ground-truth paper retrieved: NO” is a retrieval problem: a different chunk size, a reranker, or a better embedding model is the fix, and no generator will help. “Yes” with is_blank is the model declining on evidence it had, which the system prompt and the retrieval threshold control. “Yes” with a wrong value is a reading error, and the cited passage usually shows what it latched onto: a nearby number, a different unit, a different model in the same table. And sometimes the explanation shows the model read correctly and the label is the problem: a question asking what inference “can account for” labelled 90 where three papers in the corpus give 60, 70 and 80 to 90 percent, so a range is arguably the better answer, or a fact that appears in several papers with the label naming only one of them. Labels are written by people. When the explanation convinces you, the fix is to the label, and the competition organisers want to hear about it. Each of those is a different lever, and the score alone would have you pulling the wrong one.

    Challenge

    What did that run cost?

    Every converse response carried a usage block, and call_bedrock_chat kept them all in bedrock_usage. Sum the input and output tokens over the evaluation run and price them at the current on-demand rates for DeepSeek V3 on the Bedrock pricing page (fill the two prices in below). Add the embedding step: ~9,000 chunks of 1,200 characters at Titan Text Embeddings V2’s $0.02 per million input tokens. How does the total compare with the overview’s estimate for “the whole WattBot pipeline on Bedrock”, and with one hour of the ml.g6e.xlarge the Processing Jobs episode rents?

    The two prices are from the Bedrock pricing page for DeepSeek on-demand in October 2026; update them for the model and region you used. The rest sums the usage blocks and prints the cost.

    PYTHON 

    price_in_per_m = 0.62    # $ per million input tokens: DeepSeek v3.2 on-demand in us-east-2, October 2026; check the pricing page for your model and region
price_out_per_m = 1.85   # $ per million output tokens, same source

in_tokens = sum(u["inputTokens"] for u in bedrock_usage)
out_tokens = sum(u["outputTokens"] for u in bedrock_usage)
gen_cost = in_tokens / 1e6 * price_in_per_m + out_tokens / 1e6 * price_out_per_m

# Titan bills per input token; ~4 characters per token is a fair estimate for English prose
embed_tokens = sum(len(ch["text"]) for ch in chunked_docs) / 4
embed_cost = embed_tokens / 1e6 * 0.02

print(f"{len(bedrock_usage)} generation calls: {in_tokens:,} input + {out_tokens:,} output tokens -> ${gen_cost:.3f}")
print(f"~{embed_tokens:,.0f} embedding tokens -> ${embed_cost:.3f}")
print(f"Total ~${gen_cost + embed_cost:.2f}; one hour of ml.g6e.xlarge is $2.61")

    With 53 questions, two calls each and ~1,500-token prompts, the run was 140K input and 9K output tokens: ten cents at DeepSeek V3’s prices, plus five cents of embeddings for the 2.4 million tokens of corpus. All 245 questions is about half a dollar, which is the overview’s estimate for the whole pipeline, and it is a small fraction of a single GPU-hour.

    Challenge

    Swap the models

    Everything above is two model IDs and two callables. The model catalog has dozens of chat models and several embedding models, and “Choosing the two models” at the top of the episode said the leaderboards cannot tell you which one wins on your questions. Find out.

    1. A different generator. Pick another chat model from the catalog (for example us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0, us.meta.llama4-maverick-17b-instruct-v1:0, or a Mistral or Claude model if your account has access), wrap it in a tagged profile as in Step 7, and rerun the Step 11 loop on the same 55-question sample with call_bedrock_chat pointed at it. Score it with compute_wattbot_score and price it from its usage blocks. Which evidence types moved, and what did a point of score cost?
    2. A different embedder. Retrieval is the other half. Either shrink Titan to 256 dimensions ("dimensions": 256 in its request body) and see whether the hit rate and the score survive a four-times smaller index, or switch provider to Cohere Embed, if the region’s catalog offers it, whose request body is different from Titan’s: a list of texts and an input_type that is search_document for the corpus and search_query for the question. Either way the matrix must be recomputed (ten minutes at the quota, so not in class), under a new file name so the Titan one is kept.

    Keep the rest fixed. One change per experiment, or you will not know what moved the score.

    Generator. call_bedrock_chat already takes a model_id, so the swap is a profile and a lambda:

    PYTHON 

    alt_generation_model_id = "us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0"   # any chat model in the catalog with a converse API
alt_model_arn = tagged_profile_arn(bedrock, alt_generation_model_id, "wattbot-gen-alt", name, project)

usage_before = len(bedrock_usage)
alt_results = []
for _, row in eval_df.iterrows():
    alt_results.append(run_single_qa(
        row=row, embed_query=embed_query,
        generate=lambda s, u, max_new_tokens=512: call_bedrock_chat(s, u, max_new_tokens, model_id=alt_model_arn),
        chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs=chunked_docs, docid_to_url=docid_to_url,
        top_k=8, retrieval_threshold=0.25,
    ))
alt_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "wattbot_solutions_bedrock_alt.csv")
pd.DataFrame(alt_results).to_csv(alt_path, index=False)

alt_usage = bedrock_usage[usage_before:]   # only this run's calls
print(f"{sum(u['inputTokens'] for u in alt_usage):,} input + {sum(u['outputTokens'] for u in alt_usage):,} output tokens; price them from the pricing page")
compute_wattbot_score(train_qa_path=train_qa_path, preds_path=alt_path, n_examples=5)

    Read the per-type lines against the DeepSeek run. A cheaper model that holds its own on Quote questions and loses on Math and CrossPaper is the usual pattern; whether that trade is worth it depends on which questions you have.

    Embedder. First list the embedding models the region’s catalog has, because model IDs come and go and an ID that is not in the list fails at the profile step with “The provided model identifier is invalid”:

    PYTHON 

    for m in bedrock.list_foundation_models(byOutputModality="EMBEDDING")["modelSummaries"]:
    print(f"{m['modelId']:<45} {m['providerName']}")

    Titan at 256 dimensions is the same call with one more key; Cohere needs its own request and response shape. Both go through a tagged profile for the new model, and both need embed_query to use the same model as the matrix, with Cohere’s input_type switched for the question side.

    PYTHON 

    alt_embedding_model_id = base_embedding_model_id   # Titan at 256 dimensions; or a Cohere ID from the list above (cohere.embed-v4:0 where offered)
alt_embed_arn = tagged_profile_arn(bedrock, alt_embedding_model_id, "wattbot-embed-alt", name, project)

def alt_embed(text: str, for_query: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
    if "cohere" in alt_embedding_model_id:
        body = {"texts": [text[:2000]], "input_type": "search_query" if for_query else "search_document", "embedding_types": ["float"]}
    else:
        body = {"inputText": text, "dimensions": 256, "normalize": True}   # Titan Text Embeddings V2 at a quarter of the size
    out = json.loads(bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=alt_embed_arn, contentType="application/json",
                                                  accept="application/json", body=json.dumps(body))["body"].read())
    vec = out["embeddings"][0] if "embeddings" in out else out["embedding"]   # Cohere returns a list of vectors, Titan one vector
    vec = vec["float"][0] if isinstance(vec, dict) else vec                   # newer Cohere versions nest by type
    return np.asarray(vec, dtype="float32")

alt_emb_path = data_dir / "embeddings_alt.npy"   # a new file: the Titan matrix stays
if alt_emb_path.exists():
    alt_embeddings = np.load(alt_emb_path)
else:
    t0 = time.time()
    alt_embeddings = np.vstack([alt_embed(ch["text"]) for ch in chunked_docs])
    np.save(alt_emb_path, alt_embeddings)
    print(f"Embedded {len(chunked_docs)} chunks in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

alt_embed_query = lambda q: alt_embed(q, for_query=True)

    Then the Step 11 loop with embed_query=alt_embed_query and chunk_embeddings=alt_embeddings, DeepSeek unchanged, and the scorer. The hit-rate cell from Step 13 is the sharper instrument here: compute it for the new matrix before scoring, because an embedder that finds the paper less often cannot be rescued by any generator.

    Step 13 – Multimodal embeddings for the table and figure questions

    Look back at the evidence-type table in Step 12. The Table and Figure rows are usually the worst, and the reason is upstream of the model. pypdf gives us a page’s text: a table comes out as a run of numbers with its column headers somewhere else on the page, and a figure comes out as its caption and nothing more. A question whose answer is a bar in a plot has nothing in the chunks to find, and a question whose answer is a cell in a table is being read from a flattened copy.

    A multimodal embedding model is one model that maps text and images into the same vector space, so a text question can be compared with an image directly: the picture of a table lands near a sentence about its contents. Bedrock has two: Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings (text, images, documents, video and audio, released 2025) and the older Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 (text and images). Both are per-call, like Titan Text, and billed per image plus per text token; the Bedrock pricing page has the rates, on the order of a hundredth of a cent per image. One catch: in October 2026 both are offered in us-east-1 only (check the model catalog for that region). A Bedrock call is an HTTPS request and the region is a parameter, so from Ohio that is a second client pointed at Virginia; it also means the images leave the region, which is the thing to check against your institution’s data policy before doing this with documents that are not public papers.

    This step cuts the tables and figures out of the PDFs as images, builds a second index from them next to the text one, measures whether it finds the right paper for table and figure questions more often, and then hands the images to a model that can look at them. Each cell is short because the plumbing is in wattbot_rag.py.

    Extract the tables and figures

    Why cut them out at all, rather than hand the embedding model a whole page, or the PDF itself (Nova accepts documents as input)? For the same reason Step 6 cut the text into chunks instead of embedding each paper whole. An embedding is a fixed-length vector, a thousand numbers, whatever goes in; the more that goes in, the less of each thing survives in it. A page holding two tables, a figure and three paragraphs gets one vector that is a blur of all six, and a question about one of the tables has to match that blur. A crop of the table gets a vector that is about the table. The same holds at generation time: the vision model reads a crop at full resolution for a few hundred tokens, where a page costs a thousand tokens and shows the table at a quarter of the size. We tried whole pages first on this corpus; the callout at the end has the numbers, and they are the floor the crops should beat.

    A PDF has no table or figure objects to pull out. It stores text runs, raster images, and drawing commands (lines, fills, curves), and a plot is a few thousand of the last. PyMuPDF ships three detectors that turn those back into boxes: find_tables finds tables from their rulings or their text alignment, get_image_info lists the embedded raster images, and cluster_drawings groups the drawing commands of a vector figure into one bounding box. extract_figures_and_tables in wattbot_rag.py runs the three on every page, drops page-sized background fills, rules and logos, pairs each box with the nearest caption line starting “Table N” or “Figure N” (tables are captioned above, figures below) and widens the crop to include that caption, so the image carries the identifier a question will use. A caption whose box no detector found falls back to the whole page, so nothing the text mentions is missed. Open the function; it is sixty lines and every rule in it is a line you can change. The detectors are the slow part, a second or two per page on this instance, so the cell runs them only on the pages whose text carries a caption, under half of the corpus; in class, with use_instructor_embeddings set, it downloads the crops your instructor made instead.

    PYTHON 

    %pip install -q pymupdf

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import extract_figures_and_tables, find_caption_pages, embed_multimodal, image_blocks, hit_at_k

crop_dir = data_dir / "crops"
crops_path = data_dir / "crops.jsonl"
shared_crops_key = "wattbot/crops.zip"   # the instructor's crops, staged like the embeddings

if not crops_path.exists() and use_instructor_embeddings and _s3_object_exists(shared_bucket, shared_crops_key):
    s3.download_file(shared_bucket, shared_crops_key, str(data_dir / "crops.zip"))
    with zipfile.ZipFile(data_dir / "crops.zip") as zf:
        zf.extractall(data_dir)
    (data_dir / "crops.zip").unlink()
    print("Downloaded the instructor's crops")

if crops_path.exists():
    crops = [json.loads(line) for line in open(crops_path)]
else:
    caption_pages: Dict[str, Dict[int, set]] = {}   # per paper, the pages whose text carries a caption, and which kinds: the detectors run only there
    for p in find_caption_pages(page_docs):
        caption_pages.setdefault(p["doc_id"], {})[p["page_num"]] = {"table" if c.startswith("Table") else "figure" for c in p["captions"]}
    t0 = time.time()
    crops = []
    for i, (doc_id, page_nums) in enumerate(sorted(caption_pages.items())):
        crops += extract_figures_and_tables(os.path.join(PDF_DIR, f"{doc_id}.pdf"), doc_id, crop_dir, pages=page_nums)
        if (i + 1) % 10 == 0:
            print(f"{i + 1} papers, {len(crops)} crops so far ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
    with open(crops_path, "w") as f:
        f.writelines(json.dumps(c) + "\n" for c in crops)
    print(f"Extracted {len(crops)} crops from {len(caption_pages)} papers in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

n_tables = sum(c["kind"] == "table" for c in crops)
n_pages = sum(c["whole_page"] for c in crops)
print(f"{n_tables} tables and {len(crops) - n_tables} figures; {n_pages} of them are whole-page fallbacks")
crops[:3]

    Look at a few before trusting them: a crop that is a logo, a page rule, or half a plot tells you which threshold to change.

    PYTHON 

    from IPython.display import Image, display

for c in [c for c in crops if c["kind"] == "table"][:2] + [c for c in crops if c["kind"] == "figure"][:2]:
    print(f"{c['doc_id']} page {c['page_label']}: {c['caption']}")
    display(Image(filename=c["png_path"], width=500))

    Embed the crops

    The embedding model lives in us-east-1, so this is a second runtime client pointed there. One difference from the text models: Bedrock rejects this model’s request body when it arrives through an application inference profile, so these calls use the model ID directly and are the one Bedrock spend in this lesson that carries no project tags. embed_multimodal builds the model’s request body (Nova’s says whether a vector is for the index or for a query, and that the image is a document rather than a photo) and returns a unit vector. Set multimodal_model_id to amazon.titan-embed-image-v1 to try the older model; the function handles both.

    PYTHON 

    multimodal_region = "us-east-1"
multimodal_model_id = "amazon.nova-2-multimodal-embeddings-v1:0"   # called by ID: this model does not accept calls through an inference profile

bedrock_runtime_mm = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=multimodal_region,
                                  config=Config(retries={"max_attempts": 10, "mode": "adaptive"}))

v = embed_multimodal(bedrock_runtime_mm, multimodal_model_id, image_png=Path(crops[0]["png_path"]).read_bytes())
print(f"{crops[0]['doc_id']} {crops[0]['caption'][:40]!r} -> vector of {v.shape[0]} dimensions")

    One call per crop, cached like the text matrix: locally, then in your bucket, then computed. The loop runs six calls at a time through a thread pool and prints every fifty; a thousand images takes about two minutes. The question side uses the same model with purpose="query".

    PYTHON 

    crop_emb_path = data_dir / "embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy"
crop_emb_key = "wattbot/embeddings/embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy"

if crop_emb_path.exists():
    crop_embeddings = np.load(crop_emb_path)
elif use_instructor_embeddings and _s3_object_exists(shared_bucket, "wattbot/embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy"):
    s3.download_file(shared_bucket, "wattbot/embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy", str(crop_emb_path))
    crop_embeddings = np.load(crop_emb_path)
    print("Downloaded the instructor's crop embeddings")
elif _s3_object_exists(bucket_name, crop_emb_key):
    s3.download_file(bucket_name, crop_emb_key, str(crop_emb_path))
    crop_embeddings = np.load(crop_emb_path)
else:
    from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

    def embed_crop(c):
        return embed_multimodal(bedrock_runtime_mm, multimodal_model_id, image_png=Path(c["png_path"]).read_bytes())

    t0 = time.time()
    rows = []
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) as pool:   # one image per call: six in flight at a time
        for i, vec in enumerate(pool.map(embed_crop, crops)):
            rows.append(vec)
            if (i + 1) % 50 == 0:
                print(f"Embedded {i + 1} / {len(crops)} crops ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s, {(i + 1) / (time.time() - t0):.1f} per second)")
    crop_embeddings = np.vstack(rows)
    np.save(crop_emb_path, crop_embeddings)
    s3.upload_file(str(crop_emb_path), bucket_name, crop_emb_key)
    print(f"Embedded {len(crops)} crops in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

assert crop_embeddings.shape[0] == len(crops), "crop embeddings and crops are out of step; delete the cached file and rerun"
print("Crop embeddings shape:", crop_embeddings.shape)

def embed_query_mm(question: str) -> np.ndarray:
    return embed_multimodal(bedrock_runtime_mm, multimodal_model_id, text=question, purpose="query")

    Does the image index find the right paper more often?

    Retrieval is the same retrieve_top_k as Step 9, over the crop matrix instead of the chunk matrix. train_QA.csv names the paper each answer comes from, so the cleanest measure is the hit rate: the fraction of questions for which a ground-truth paper is among the top-k results. Higher is better, and 1.00 means every question had the right paper in front of the model. We compute it for the text index and the image index on the Table questions, the Figure questions and, as a control, the Quote questions, where the image index should have no advantage.

    PYTHON 

    k = 8
groups = {"Table": train_df[train_df["Table"] == 1], "Figure": train_df[train_df["Figure"] == 1],
          "Quote only": train_df[(train_df["Quote"] == 1) & (train_df["Table"] == 0) & (train_df["Figure"] == 0)].head(40)}

print("Hit rate at k=8 (higher is better): share of questions whose ground-truth paper is in the top 8 results\n")
print(f"{'questions':<12}{'n':>4}{'text index':>14}{'image index':>14}")
for label, qs in groups.items():
    gt = [split_ref_ids(r) for r in qs["ref_id"]]
    text_hits = [[c["doc_id"] for c in retrieve_top_k(embed_query(q), chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs, k=k)] for q in qs["question"]]
    image_hits = [[c["doc_id"] for c in retrieve_top_k(embed_query_mm(q), crop_embeddings, crops, k=k)] for q in qs["question"]]
    print(f"{label:<12}{len(qs):>4}{hit_at_k(text_hits, gt):>14.2f}{hit_at_k(image_hits, gt):>14.2f}")

    Two numbers per row, higher is better, and three readings. If the image index wins on Table and Figure and ties on Quote, the embedding model is doing what it was built for. If it loses everywhere, look at what it was given: a crop of a dense table at 150 dpi is readable, a cropped panel of a nine-panel figure may not be, and a whole-page fallback is a weak key. If both indexes already find the paper for nearly every question, retrieval was never the problem for this corpus and the loss is in the reading, which the next cells test.

    Let the model see the table or figure

    Finding the table is half of it; DeepSeek V3 reads text only, so a figure retrieved as an image is no use to it. converse accepts image blocks in a user message for models that can see, and the swap is the model ID: Amazon Nova 2 Lite reads images and documents and is in the catalog for Ohio through the cross-region profile below (check the model catalog; us.amazon.nova-lite-v1:0 is the cheaper, weaker alternative). call_vision_chat is call_bedrock_chat with an images argument: for each attached crop it adds a text label naming the paper and the caption, then the image, so the model can cite what it reads.

    PYTHON 

    base_vision_model_id = "us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0"
vision_model_id = tagged_profile_arn(bedrock, base_vision_model_id, "wattbot-vision", name, project)
vision_usage = []

def call_vision_chat(system_prompt: str, user_prompt: str, max_new_tokens: int = 512, images=()) -> str:
    """One system + user turn, with zero or more (label, png_bytes) images attached to the user turn."""
    content = [{"text": user_prompt}]
    if images:
        content.append({"text": "The images below are tables and figures from the same papers; read values from them where the text above is incomplete."})
        content.extend(image_blocks(images))
    response = bedrock_runtime.converse(
        modelId=vision_model_id,
        system=[{"text": system_prompt}],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}],
        inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": max_new_tokens, "temperature": 0},
    )
    vision_usage.append(response["usage"])
    return "\n".join(b["text"] for b in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in b).strip()

def crop_label(c) -> str:
    return f"{c['doc_id']}, page {c['page_label']}, {c['caption'][:60]}" if c["caption"] else f"{c['doc_id']}, page {c['page_label']}"

print(call_vision_chat("You are a concise assistant.", "What is in the attached image? One sentence.", 64,
                       images=[(crop_label(crops[0]), Path(crops[0]["png_path"]).read_bytes())]))

    Three runs over the Table and Figure questions, all through the vision model, so that the only thing changing between them is what the model is shown. The first is the control: text chunks only. The second attaches the top three crops from the image index. The third attaches the crops from the pages the top text chunks came from: if the hit-rate table says the text index is the better finder, the question is whether finding with text and reading with the image is the better split. Each run is the same loop as Step 11, so every question costs an answer call and an explanation call.

    PYTHON 

    tf_df = train_df[(train_df["Table"] == 1) | (train_df["Figure"] == 1)]
crops_by_page: Dict[tuple, list] = {}
for c in crops:
    crops_by_page.setdefault((c["doc_id"], c["page_num"]), []).append(c)
print(f"{len(tf_df)} table and figure questions; each run makes an answer call and an explanation call per question, so about {6 * len(tf_df)} calls for three runs")

def crops_for(question: str, images_from: str):
    """The crops to attach: none, the image index's top three, or those on the pages behind the top text chunks."""
    if images_from == "image_index":
        return retrieve_top_k(embed_query_mm(question), crop_embeddings, crops, k=3)
    if images_from == "text_index":
        found = []
        for ch in retrieve_top_k(embed_query(question), chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs, k=8):
            for c in crops_by_page.get((ch["doc_id"], ch["page_num"]), []):
                if c not in found:
                    found.append(c)
        return found[:3]
    return []

def run_tf(images_from: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for _, row in tf_df.iterrows():
        images = [(crop_label(c), Path(c["png_path"]).read_bytes()) for c in crops_for(row["question"], images_from)]
        generate = lambda s, u, max_new_tokens=512, images=images: call_vision_chat(s, u, max_new_tokens, images=images)
        rows.append(run_single_qa(row=row, embed_query=embed_query, generate=generate, chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,
                                  chunked_docs=chunked_docs, docid_to_url=docid_to_url, top_k=8, retrieval_threshold=0.25))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

vision_runs = {"text chunks only": "none", "chunks + crops from the image index": "image_index", "chunks + crops behind the text chunks": "text_index"}
t0 = time.time()
for label, images_from in vision_runs.items():
    run_tf(images_from).to_csv(os.path.join(output_dir, f"wattbot_solutions_vision_{images_from}.csv"), index=False)
    print(f"{label}: done at {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

    Score all three the same way as Step 12. The scorer compares the rows it finds, so the breakdown is over these questions only; the Table and Figure lines are the ones to read, across the three runs and against the DeepSeek run.

    PYTHON 

    for label, images_from in vision_runs.items():
    print("=" * 96)
    print(f"Nova 2 Lite, {label}")
    compute_wattbot_score(train_qa_path=train_qa_path, preds_path=os.path.join(output_dir, f"wattbot_solutions_vision_{images_from}.csv"), n_examples=3)
    Callout

    What to expect, and what it cost

    Measured once on this corpus with whole page images rather than crops, on 50 table and figure questions, before the extraction step above was written; the crops should do better, and the numbers here are the floor. Retrieval first: the text index found a ground-truth paper in its top eight for 94% of the table questions and 94% of the figure questions; the page-image index managed 91% and 82%. A whole page is a weaker key than the caption and surrounding sentences that the text chunks already carry. Then reading: with the image index’s top three pages attached, Nova 2 Lite went from 0.64 to 0.67 overall, from 41% to 29% of figure questions wrong, and from 0.85 to 0.93 on citation F1, while the table questions did not move (43% to 46% wrong). Seventeen figure questions is two questions of difference, so read the direction, not the decimals. For the bill, every image is a few hundred to a thousand input tokens at Nova 2 Lite’s rate on the pricing page, so a run with images costs two to three times the control; vision_usage holds all three runs’ usage blocks, and the embedding of the crops is the per-image rate times len(crops), a few cents. The three runs together take about eight minutes.

    Wrap‑up: Bedrock versus GPU‑based runs

    You now have a complete WattBot evaluation running on Bedrock, with per‑token billing and nothing left running. The Processing Jobs episode reruns the same evaluation on a self‑hosted model, and the optional GPU-notebook episode does it once more interactively, so by the end you will have three versions to compare:

    1. Bedrock (this episode) using hosted embedding and generation models with per‑token billing.
    2. SageMaker Processing job running an open‑source model in batch with on-demand compute.
    3. Notebook GPU instance (optional) using the same locally loaded open‑source model.

    When deciding between these options in practice:

    • Use Bedrock or other hosted APIs when:
      • You want to try the latest frontier models quickly.
      • You only need to run a modest number of questions, or you are still prototyping.
      • You prefer a simple, token‑based cost model and don’t want to manage GPU capacity.
    • Use self‑hosted models on GPU instances when:
      • You need a specific open-weight model that the catalog does not carry.
      • You expect to run large batches repeatedly (e.g., many thousands of questions).
      • You want tight control over which architectures/checkpoints you run or fine‑tune.
      • You already have institutional access to cost‑effective on‑prem or cloud GPUs.

    The core RAG evaluation logic stays identical across all three episodes, which is the main takeaway: once you have a clean retrieval + normalization pipeline (like WattBot’s, in wattbot_rag.py), swapping out the generator is mostly a matter of re‑implementing embed_query and generate for each compute option you care about.

    Concluding remarks: Bedrock models are one piece of the RAG puzzle

    In this episode we used Bedrock-hosted models for both embedding and generation. Larger, higher-quality models can definitely help a ton — especially on messy real-world questions — but it’s important to remember that they are still just one component in your RAG system.

    • Bigger or newer models do not magically fix weak retrieval. If your chunks are poorly aligned with the questions, a very strong LLM will still struggle.
    • Most of the long‑term accuracy gains in RAG systems come from the plumbing around the LLMs, including:
      • smarter / semantic chunking strategies
      • good metadata and filtering
      • reranking or multi‑stage retrieval
      • domain‑specific heuristics and post‑processing
    • Cost and latency live in tension with quality. Larger models (or higher token budgets) often improve answers, but at the cost of more inference time and higher per‑request spend. Bedrock makes it easier to experiment with that tradeoff by switching models without rewriting your pipeline.

    As you adapt this notebook to your own projects, treat the LLM choice as one tunable component in a larger system. Iterating on chunking, indexing, and retrieval policies will almost always give you more headroom than swapping between already-good models.

    Key Points
    • A complete RAG pipeline on AWS needs no GPU: a CPU notebook plus Bedrock-hosted embedding and generation models is enough.
    • Corpus preparation (unpacking the staged PDFs, page extraction, chunking) is cheap CPU work; cache chunks.jsonl on S3 so later episodes and runs can reuse it.
    • Bedrock calls carry no tags; route them through a tagged application inference profile or the spend is anonymous on the bill.
    • converse is the provider-neutral way to call a chat model on Bedrock; its usage block is what you are billed on. DeepSeek V3 is the generator here, and any catalog model is a one-line swap.
    • Bedrock bills per token and leaves nothing running between calls, which is why it is the default route for RAG inference.
    • The model is one tunable component; most accuracy gains come from chunking, retrieval, and post-processing.

    Content from RAG with Processing Jobs

    Last updated on 2026-10-21 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • When does a RAG pipeline need a self-hosted, open-weight model instead of Bedrock, and what is the safest way to rent the GPU for it?
    • How do we run the embedding and generation steps of the WattBot pipeline as SageMaker Processing jobs that end on their own?
    • How do we pass data in and out of a job through S3, and tag the job so its cost is traceable?

    Objectives

    • Explain why Bedrock’s catalog is not enough when you need a specific open-weight model, and why a Processing job is the default way to self-host one for batch work.
    • Launch a GPU Processing job that embeds the cached WattBot chunks with a self-hosted embedding model and writes the vectors to S3.
    • Launch a second Processing job that runs Qwen3-8B (an open-weight model in a size Bedrock does not carry) with transformers and runs the full RAG loop over the training questions.
    • Read a job’s inputs, outputs, arguments and runtime cap, and relate its duration to what it cost.
    • Score the batch predictions with the WattBot metric and compare against the Bedrock run.

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/12_RAG-Processing-jobs.ipynb. Select the conda_pytorch kernel. ## When Bedrock does not have your model

    The Bedrock episode is the default for RAG: per-token billing, nothing left running, two API calls. Bedrock’s catalog is curated, though. It carries Amazon’s models, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, and a few others, and within a family only some sizes, usually a generation behind: for Qwen, the serverless lineup is still the Qwen3 series. Hugging Face hosts well over a million open-weight checkpoints. The one you want (the newest release, a specific size, a fine-tune for scientific text, a model a paper just published) is usually not on Bedrock, and often never will be.

    When that happens you host the model yourself on a GPU you rent, and the question becomes how. There are three ways to rent a GPU on SageMaker:

    Bills Stops when Best for
    GPU notebook instance by the hour from start to stop you stop it interactive debugging, prototyping at the keyboard
    Processing or training job by the second while the job runs the script ends, or max_runtime_in_seconds batch work: embed a corpus, answer a list of questions, train
    Inference endpoint by the hour while deployed you delete it serving a model to an application with steady traffic

    For research RAG, almost all the work is batch: embed everything once, answer a list of questions, score them. That is a job, and a job is the one option that cannot be forgotten. This episode runs the WattBot pipeline that way. The notebook itself is a small CPU instance and never touches the model; it stages data, launches two GPU jobs, and reads the results back.

    The generator is Qwen3-8B, an 8-billion-parameter open-weight model (Apache 2.0). Bedrock serves the 32B and 235B members of that family but not this size, which is the usual situation: the size you want is the one missing. The job runs it with transformers, the same library the fine-tuning episode trained with: from_pretrained downloads the weights onto the GPU, and generate writes the answer to a chat prompt, the self-hosted counterpart of what Bedrock does behind converse. Inference needs no gradients, so the weights are the memory cost: 8B parameters at two bytes each in bf16 is about 16 GB, which fits the 24 GB GPU of an ml.g5.xlarge with room for the KV cache. (The fine-tuning episode has the full memory arithmetic; the short version is that inference needs only the weights and training needs eight times more per parameter.)

    Why bother serving a model yourself when Bedrock is a call away? Because open-weight models that fit one GPU are now close to the frontier on the kinds of tasks research code runs, on data that never leaves your account. The newest of this family, Qwen3.8-27B, fits one GPU and lands within a few points of a frontier commercial model:

    Qwen figures are from the Qwen3.8-27B model card and were not reproduced here; Opus 4.8 figures are from its published evaluations.

    Callout

    What this episode costs

    Job Instance $/h Expected duration Cost
    Embed ~9,000 chunks ml.g5.xlarge (A10G, 24 GB) $1.41 ~10 min incl. startup ~$0.20
    RAG over a 53-question sample with Qwen3-8B ml.g5.xlarge (A10G, 24 GB) $1.41 ~20 min: 1 provisioning, ~4 downloading and loading 16 GB of weights, ~13 generating ~$0.40
    Controller notebook ml.t3.medium $0.05 2 h $0.10

    About $0.70 for the episode, and the GPUs are off the moment each script ends. The RAG job answers the same stratified sample of questions as the Bedrock episode (ten per evidence type, 53 questions once the two papers the corpus lacks are dropped); all 220 is about an hour of generation, so run that at home. Both jobs carry max_runtime_in_seconds, so a hung job costs at most the cap. Compare the same pipeline on a GPU notebook instance (the optional GPU-notebook episode at the end of the lesson): the meter runs until someone stops it, and a forgotten ml.g5.xlarge is $34 a day.

    The trade-off is latency. A job takes minutes to start, so this pattern is for batch questions, not a chatbot. For interactive use, Bedrock answers in seconds; for interactive use of a model Bedrock does not have, an inference endpoint does, at an hourly rate you have to remember to turn off.

    In this episode we will:

    • Reuse the chunks cached in your bucket by the Bedrock episode and the inputs in the shared bucket.
    • Run two short-lived GPU Processing jobs: one computes embeddings for all chunks; the second runs Qwen3-8B with transformers and the full RAG loop (retrieval + generation) over all training questions.
    • Score the result and compare it with the Bedrock run.

    Setup

    The scripts

    Jobs run in containers, so the code they execute has to be shipped with the job: a Processing job cannot import functions defined in this notebook. The lesson repository has the three files we need as standalone scripts. Clone it:

    • scripts/embedding_inference.py: generic embedding script (JSONL with a text field in, embeddings.npy out).
    • scripts/hf_embedder.py: the embedding model wrapper both jobs use, on plain transformers (mean pooling and normalisation, thirty lines), so neither job has to install anything for it.
    • scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py: the WattBot RAG loop as a batch job: loads the inputs, runs the generator, writes wattbot_solutions.csv.
    • scripts/wattbot_rag.py: the shared pipeline logic (retrieval, prompts, answer parsing, run_single_qa, the scorer) that the Bedrock episode imported too. The batch script imports it, so it ships with the job; the notebook imports it for scoring.

    The cell below copies them out of the lesson clone into the project folder, one directory per job: code_embed/ for the embedding job and code_rag/ for the RAG job. The split follows from how a job gets its code. run(source_dir=...) uploads that whole directory into the container, the same way the training estimator’s source_dir did in the fine-tuning episode, so each directory holds exactly the files its job imports. The copies of wattbot_rag.py and Score.py next to the notebook are for the scoring step at the end, which runs in the notebook, not in a job.

    PYTHON 

    !mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/wattbot   # the same project folder the Bedrock episode used, beside the lesson clone
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/wattbot

# One source directory per job: SageMaker uploads the whole directory into the container
!mkdir -p code_embed code_rag
# The embedding job's script
!cp /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/embedding_inference.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/hf_embedder.py code_embed/
# The RAG job's script plus the shared module it imports (the container cannot see this notebook)
!cp /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/hf_embedder.py code_rag/
# The notebook's own copies, for scoring at the end: the pipeline module and the competition's metric file
!cp /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/Score.py .
!ls code_embed code_rag

    Next, set up the AWS SDK, SageMaker session, and bucket names.

    PYTHON 

    import os
import json

import boto3
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sagemaker
from sagemaker import get_execution_role
from sagemaker.huggingface import HuggingFaceProcessor         # launches a job in the prebuilt Hugging Face container
from sagemaker.processing import ProcessingInput, ProcessingOutput   # S3 <-> container path mappings for a job

session = sagemaker.Session()
region = session.boto_region_name
role = get_execution_role()   # the IAM role the jobs run under to read and write S3

shared_bucket = "ml-marathon-shared"   # the instructor-staged, read-only bucket with the data and model weights; change only on your own account
bucket_name = "sinkorswim-doejohn"     # <-- EDIT ME: your own bucket (chunks in, outputs out)
s3_client = boto3.client("s3", region_name=region)

local_data_dir = "./data"
os.makedirs(local_data_dir, exist_ok=True)

print("Region:", region)
print("Role:", role)
print("Bucket:", bucket_name)

    Step 1 – Check the inputs

    The jobs read three files from S3: train_QA.csv and metadata.csv from the shared bucket, and chunks.jsonl from your bucket, where the Bedrock episode cached it. The PDFs themselves are not needed again: chunking was done once, and the jobs work from the chunks. We download the three files to the notebook only to confirm they exist and to look at them; the jobs fetch their own copies from S3.

    First the keys and the full S3 URIs. The URIs are the form a ProcessingInput takes, so they are built here once and reused when the jobs are launched.

    PYTHON 

    train_qa_key = "wattbot/train_QA.csv"
metadata_key = "wattbot/metadata.csv"
chunks_s3_key = "wattbot/chunks.jsonl"

# Full S3 URIs: this is the form a ProcessingInput takes
train_qa_s3 = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{train_qa_key}"
metadata_s3 = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{metadata_key}"
chunks_s3_uri = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{chunks_s3_key}"

def smart_read_csv(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a CSV as utf-8, falling back to latin-1 for the odd accented author name."""
    try:
        return pd.read_csv(path)
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        return pd.read_csv(path, encoding="latin-1")

    Then download the three files, skipping any already on disk, and load them so we can check the counts before spending GPU time on them.

    PYTHON 

    train_qa_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "train_QA.csv")
metadata_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "metadata.csv")
local_chunks_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "chunks.jsonl")

if not os.path.exists(train_qa_path):
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, train_qa_key, train_qa_path)
if not os.path.exists(metadata_path):
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, metadata_key, metadata_path)
if not os.path.exists(local_chunks_path):
    s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, chunks_s3_key, local_chunks_path)   # written by the Bedrock episode

train_df = smart_read_csv(train_qa_path)
metadata_df = smart_read_csv(metadata_path)
with open(local_chunks_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    chunked_docs = [json.loads(line) for line in f]

print("Train QAs:", len(train_df))
print("Metadata rows:", len(metadata_df))
print("Chunks:", len(chunked_docs), "from", chunks_s3_uri)
train_df.head(3)

    If the last download fails with NoSuchKey, go back to the Bedrock episode and run its chunking step; this episode starts from its output.

    Step 2 – Processing Job 1: embed all chunks on a GPU

    Now we launch a short-lived Hugging Face Processing job that:

    1. Downloads chunks.jsonl from S3.
    2. Loads thenlper/gte-large from Hugging Face with the container’s own transformers.
    3. Encodes each chunk into an embedding vector.
    4. Saves the full matrix as embeddings.npy back to S3.

    We use the same embedding_inference.py script across projects; here it expects a JSONL file with a text field.

    Nothing to install

    Neither job installs anything. The Hugging Face container ships transformers and PyTorch, which is all the embedding wrapper and the generator need, so both jobs start as soon as the instance is up. A requirements.txt next to a script would be pip-installed before it runs; neither job here has one.

    Callout

    Why not vLLM?

    vLLM is the open-source inference engine most people serve open-weight models with: you give it a model name, it loads the weights onto the GPU and answers chat requests, batching many at once so that throughput scales. That is what you want behind an API with users. This job sends about 100 prompts one at a time, so the batching would go unused, and the install is several gigabytes of billed GPU time. transformers.generate, already in the container, does the same prompts in about thirteen minutes with nothing to install. The GPU-notebook episode uses vLLM, where its 8-bit weights are needed to fit a larger model.

    Cost tracking: tag every job

    Tags do not propagate in AWS. The tags you put on your notebook instance cover the notebook’s hourly cost and nothing else. Each Processing job below launches its own GPU instance, which is a separate billable resource with no tags unless we pass them at launch, exactly as we did for training and tuning jobs earlier in the workshop. An untagged job shows up in Cost Explorer as anonymous SageMaker spend that nobody can attribute to a team.

    Define the tags once and pass tags=job_tags to every HuggingFaceProcessor you create. Use a distinct Purpose per job so you can tell the embedding job from the batch RAG job on the bill.

    PYTHON 

    name = "DoeJohn"         # replace with your name
project = "SinkOrSwim"   # replace with your challenge name

def make_job_tags(purpose: str):   # one of: Storage, Notebook, Training, Tuning, Inference
    return [
        {"Key": "Name", "Value": name},
        {"Key": "Project", "Value": project},
        {"Key": "Purpose", "Value": purpose},   # differs per job so the bill tells them apart
    ]

    Launch the embedding job

    Open scripts/embedding_inference.py first; it is under fifty lines. It reads a JSONL file of chunks from the job’s input directory, embeds them with whatever Hugging Face model --model_id names, through the thirty-line wrapper in hf_embedder.py, normalises the vectors so a dot product is a cosine similarity, and saves one embeddings.npy to the output directory. Nothing in it knows about WattBot, which is the point of a Processing job script: inputs in, outputs out, no state.

    A HuggingFaceProcessor is the Processing-job counterpart of the estimator: the same role, tags, instance type and container versions, plus a runtime cap. Its run call names the script, mounts the inputs, and says where the output goes. Once it is launched, the job appears on the Processing jobs page of the SageMaker console (under Data preparation in the left menu), the Processing counterpart of the Training jobs page you used earlier.

    In class the instructor has run this job already and staged its output. The switch below copies that matrix into your bucket, at the key the job would have written, and the launch cell then skips the job: the second job, which you do launch, has the same shape and is where the class spends its GPU minutes. On your own, set it to False and run the job; it is eight minutes.

    PYTHON 

    def _s3_object_exists(bucket: str, key: str) -> bool:
    try:
        s3_client.head_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)
        return True
    except s3_client.exceptions.ClientError:
        return False

embedding_model_id = "thenlper/gte-large"
emb_output_prefix = "wattbot/embeddings"
emb_output_path = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/"

use_instructor_embeddings = True                       # True in class: copy the instructor's gte-large matrix and skip the job. False: run the job
shared_gte_key = "wattbot/embeddings_gte_large.npy"    # where the instructor staged it in the shared bucket

run_embedding_job = not (use_instructor_embeddings and _s3_object_exists(shared_bucket, shared_gte_key))
if not run_embedding_job:
    s3_client.copy({"Bucket": shared_bucket, "Key": shared_gte_key}, bucket_name, f"{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy")
    print(f"Copied the instructor's embeddings to s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy; the embedding job is skipped")

    PYTHON 

    
embedding_processor = HuggingFaceProcessor(
    base_job_name="WattBot-embed-gte-large",   # SageMaker appends a timestamp to make each job name unique
    role=role,
    tags=make_job_tags("Inference"),   # tags are per job; nothing is inherited from the notebook
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge",      # the GPU the job rents (A10G, 24 GB): plenty for a 335M-parameter embedder
    instance_count=1,
    transformers_version="4.56",       # these three pick the prebuilt container image
    pytorch_version="2.8",
    py_version="py312",
    sagemaker_session=session,
    max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60,   # 2 hours, in seconds (2 h x 60 min x 60 s); the estimate is ~8 minutes. SageMaker kills the job here, so a hang costs at most this
)

if run_embedding_job:   # False in class when the instructor's matrix was copied in above
    # run() uploads the code, starts the instance, streams the job's log here and returns when the script ends (wait=True is the default)
    start = time.time()
    embedding_processor.run(
        code="embedding_inference.py",     # the script the container runs...
        source_dir="code_embed/",          # ...uploaded with everything beside it (hf_embedder.py)
        inputs=[
            ProcessingInput(
                source=chunks_s3_uri,                       # S3 object (or prefix) copied in before the script starts
                destination="/opt/ml/processing/input",    # where it appears inside the container
            )
        ],
        outputs=[
            ProcessingOutput(
                output_name="embeddings",
                source="/opt/ml/processing/output",        # whatever the script writes here...
                destination=emb_output_path,               # ...is copied to this S3 prefix when the script ends
            )
        ],
        arguments=[                        # command-line flags, as the script's argparse expects them
            "--model_id", embedding_model_id,
            "--input_filename", "chunks.jsonl",
            "--text_key", "text",
            "--input_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/input",
            "--output_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/output",
        ],
    )

    print(f"Embedding job complete: {(time.time() - start) / 60:.1f} min wall-clock, including instance startup")

    Check on the running job in the AWS Console

    To view the job running from the AWS Console, you can visit SageMaker AI, and then find the “Data Preparation” dropdown menu on the left side panel. Click that to find “Processing jobs”, or open this link in the class region (change us-east-2 in it for another region).

    It takes about 10 minutes in total for the job to complete: a couple of provisioning the instance and downloading the embedding model, eight of embedding. This is the downside of launching jobs, but the good news is that we only need to launch one embedding job for our RAG pipeline. This strategy also ensures we’re only paying for the GPU while the job runs.

    Sanity-check the embeddings locally

    We can download embeddings.npy back into the notebook and inspect its shape to confirm the job ran successfully.

    PYTHON 

    local_embeddings_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "embeddings.npy")
embeddings_key = f"{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy"   # the ProcessingOutput destination + the filename the script wrote

s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, embeddings_key, local_embeddings_path)
chunk_embeddings = np.load(local_embeddings_path)

print("Embeddings shape:", chunk_embeddings.shape, "for", len(chunked_docs), "chunks")

    Step 3 – Processing Job 2: full WattBot RAG over all questions

    For the second job, we pass four inputs:

    • chunks.jsonl – serialized chunks (your bucket)
    • embeddings.npy – precomputed chunk embeddings (your bucket, written by Job 1)
    • train_QA.csv – training questions (shared bucket)
    • metadata.csv – to resolve ref_id → URL (shared bucket)

    The --per_type 10 argument draws the same stratified sample the Bedrock episode scored, ten questions per evidence type with the same seed, so the two runs are compared on the same questions; leave it out to answer them all. Open scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py and read main before launching it. It is short, because the pipeline lives in scripts/wattbot_rag.py, the same module the Bedrock episode imported:

    • retrieve_top_k: cosine similarity over the embedding matrix
    • run_single_qa: retrieval, the answer call, the hybrid unanswerable rule (retrieval threshold OR the model’s own is_blank), the explanation call
    • compute_wattbot_score: the metric we use at the end

    What the batch script adds is the two model callables: embed_query wraps the same gte-large model and pooling the embedding job used (hf_embedder.py) (the question has to be embedded with the same model as the chunks), and generate wraps transformers.generate on the generator (Qwen3-8B here) with Qwen’s thinking mode off. The job writes wattbot_solutions.csv in the WattBot submission format.

    PYTHON 

    emb_output_s3 = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy"

print("chunks:    ", chunks_s3_uri)
print("embeddings:", emb_output_s3)
print("train_QA:  ", train_qa_s3)
print("metadata:  ", metadata_s3)

    If the launch below fails at once with ResourceLimitExceeded naming an instance type, nothing in the notebook is wrong: the account’s quota for that type is too low, and the increase is requested in Service Quotas (days, for GPU types). On your own account, request ml.g5.xlarge for processing job usage before you start.

    Two settings on this processor matter more than on the embedding job. volume_size_in_gb=60 attaches a 60 GB volume to the instance, mounted under /opt/ml/processing; the container’s own root disk is small, so the 16 GB of model weights must not land there. env={"HF_HOME": ...} points Hugging Face’s download cache at that volume, which is where the weights go.

    PYTHON 

    rag_output_prefix = "wattbot/solutions"
rag_output_path = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{rag_output_prefix}/"

generation_model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3-8B"   # open-weight; Bedrock has the 32B and 235B, not this size. ~16 GB in bf16

rag_processor = HuggingFaceProcessor(
    base_job_name="WattBot-rag-batch",
    role=role,
    tags=make_job_tags("Inference"),   # separate job, separate tags
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge",      # 1 x A10G, 24 GB: holds the bf16 8B model plus KV cache
    instance_count=1,
    volume_size_in_gb=60,              # 16 GB of weights; mounted at /opt/ml/processing
    env={"HF_HOME": "/opt/ml/processing/hf_cache"},   # put the weight download on that volume
    transformers_version="4.56",
    pytorch_version="2.8",
    py_version="py312",
    sagemaker_session=session,
    max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60,   # 2 hours, in seconds; the estimate is 20 minutes
)

start = time.time()
rag_processor.run(
    code="wattbot_rag_batch.py",
    source_dir="code_rag/",            # wattbot_rag_batch.py + wattbot_rag.py + hf_embedder.py
    inputs=[
        ProcessingInput(
            source=chunks_s3_uri,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/chunks",   # four inputs, each in its own subdirectory
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=emb_output_s3,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/embeddings",
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=train_qa_s3,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/train",
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=metadata_s3,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/metadata",
        ),
    ],
    outputs=[
        ProcessingOutput(
            output_name="solutions",
            source="/opt/ml/processing/output",
            destination=rag_output_path,
        )
    ],
    arguments=[
        "--input_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/input",
        "--output_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/output",
        "--embedding_model_id", embedding_model_id,
        "--qwen_model_id", generation_model_id,
        "--top_k", "8",
        "--retrieval_threshold", "0.25",
        "--per_type", "10",            # the same stratified sample the Bedrock episode scored (seed 0); drop it for all 245 questions
    ],
)

print(f"RAG batch job complete: {(time.time() - start) / 60:.1f} min wall-clock, including instance startup and the weight download")

    While it runs, read what the container is printing. Open the Processing jobs page, click the job’s name, scroll to Monitor and click View logs. That opens CloudWatch, the AWS service that stores every job’s printed output, at a list with one entry named after your job; click it. The text is the container’s stdout, kept after the job ends, updated while it runs (refresh). You will see, in order: the weight download (16 GB in shards), Loading model with transformers, then one line per question. The whole job is the 20 minutes in the cost callout; the generation is the second half of it.

    Step 4 – Download predictions and evaluate

    Finally, we download wattbot_solutions.csv from S3, inspect a few rows, and compute the WattBot score against train_QA.csv with the same compute_wattbot_score the Bedrock episode used.

    PYTHON

s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, solutions_key, local_solutions_path)
solutions_df = pd.read_csv(local_solutions_path)
solutions_df.head()

    Score the predictions with the competition’s own Score.py, through the same wrapper the Bedrock episode used, so the two runs compare directly.

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import compute_wattbot_score

results_df = compute_wattbot_score(
    train_qa_path=train_qa_path,
